modules.title: About Tinnitus
modules.purpose: Tinnitus is shaped by your body, mind, and daily life, not sound alone.
modules.overviewMarkdown: Tinnitus often feels like it is only about the sound: the ringing, buzzing, hissing, pulsing, or other noise that will not seem to turn off. That sound is real, and it can be distressing. But the experience of tinnitus is also shaped by what is happening in your body, your mind, and your daily life. This section introduces that bigger picture so the rest of the app makes sense.

cards.title: Seeing the whole picture
cards.bodyMarkdown: It is natural to focus on the sound first. When tinnitus feels loud or intrusive, it can seem like everything would be better if the sound simply disappeared. Sound matters, and sound therapy is still one of the core tools we will use. But tinnitus distress often grows when other parts of life get pulled into the cycle: poor sleep, stress, fear, frustration, avoidance, and feeling misunderstood. Looking at the whole picture gives you more places to make useful change.

cards.title: Why go beyond the sound?
cards.bodyMarkdown: If tinnitus were only a hearing issue, then adding more sound would solve the whole problem. Many people do benefit from hearing aids, background sound, or other sound therapy tools, but those tools may not fully address the emotional and lifestyle impact of tinnitus. That does not mean sound therapy doesn’t work. It means tinnitus is being influenced by more than one system. The goal is not to find one perfect fix. The goal is to learn which parts of the experience you can influence, then build a plan around those levers.

cards.title: Body: hearing, sound, and the nervous system
cards.bodyMarkdown: The body side of tinnitus includes the physical and medical parts of tinnitus. This may include hearing loss, noise exposure, aging, medication effects, injury, jaw or neck factors, or changes in how the auditory system and nervous system respond to sound. Sound therapy and hearing care live here because they change what the ears and brain are receiving. If hearing loss is present, audiology care and appropriate amplification can be a major part of tinnitus management.

cards.title: Mind: attention, emotion, and meaning
cards.bodyMarkdown: The mind side of tinnitus includes your reactions to tinnitus: attention, worry, fear, frustration, self-talk, and the meaning your brain attaches to the sound. This is not saying tinnitus is imaginary. The sound is real. The point is that your reaction to the sound can make it feel more threatening, more intrusive, or harder to live with. Skills like mindfulness, distress tolerance, cognitive reframing, acceptance, and self-compassion all work with this part of the tinnitus experience.

cards.title: Life: sleep, routines, relationships, and the world around you
cards.bodyMarkdown: The life side of tinnitus includes the ways tinnitus changes your day-to-day routines and relationships. You might avoid quiet rooms, skip social events, struggle at work, feel misunderstood, or notice that sleep becomes more stressful. These are not small side issues. They are part of how tinnitus becomes dominant. Communication skills, sleep education, sound planning, and gradual re-engagement help you keep your life from shrinking around tinnitus.

cards.title: What “multimodal” means
cards.bodyMarkdown: Multimodal simply means using more than one type of tool. Sound therapy can help with the sound environment. Mindfulness can help with attention. Distress tolerance can help with difficult moments. Cognitive reframing can help with thoughts that jump too far too fast. Sleep tools, self-compassion, and communication skills can help with the parts of life that tinnitus disrupts. No single tool has to do everything. Each tool gives you another way to influence the experience.

cards.title: How to use this app
cards.bodyMarkdown: This app is a guided educational companion. You can read, listen, practice, and come back to sections when you need them. The best way to begin is to understand the big picture, then start with sound therapy because it is often the most concrete first step. From there, the other sections build tools for attention, difficult moments, thoughts, sleep, self-support, and communication. You do not need to master everything at once.

cards.title: When extra support can help
cards.bodyMarkdown: Self-guided tools can be powerful, but they are not always easy to apply on your own. If you feel like you need individual help, feel confused, stuck, unsafe, or overwhelmed, support from an audiologist, ENT, mental health professional, sleep specialist, or other qualified clinician may be important. Getting help is not a failure. It is one of the ways people make these tools easier to use and more specific to their own situation.

cards.title: Small efforts can build control
cards.bodyMarkdown: Using these skills takes effort, and that can feel discouraging when tinnitus is already stressful. The goal is not to do everything perfectly. The goal is to test small strategies, notice what helps, and build a plan that gives you more influence over your day. Consistent sound use, gentle habit changes, a calmer response to thoughts, and short moments of mindfulness can all become evidence that tinnitus does not have to dominate every part of life.

cards.title: Pause & Reflect: Why am I doing this?
cards.bodyMarkdown: Before you start learning tools, take a moment to name your reason for being here. Are you looking for relief, understanding, better sleep, more confidence, or a way to make everyday life feel easier? Then imagine six months from now. How would you want tinnitus to feel different, not only in sound, but in how it affects your experience? Finally, choose one small step you can take this week. Naming your why can make the rest of the work feel more connected to your life.

cards.title: Body / Mind / Life Exploration
cards.bodyMarkdown: This exercise helps you sort your tinnitus experience into three areas. Body includes physical or medical factors, such as hearing changes, sound sensitivity, injury, or other health issues. Mind includes thoughts, emotions, stress, and worry. Life includes routines, sleep, relationships, work, and environments. A few words in each area is enough. The purpose is not to diagnose yourself. The purpose is to see the whole picture and identify where a useful next step might be.

cards.title: Main points before you move on
cards.bodyMarkdown: Tinnitus is more than sound. The sound matters, but stress, attention, sleep, thoughts, avoidance, and social life can all change how tinnitus feels. Looking at tinnitus through Body, Mind, and Life gives you more than one place to intervene. This app can be used on your own, but professional support can help when the skills feel difficult or when medical, hearing, sleep, or mental health concerns need attention. You do not need to solve everything today. Start with one useful step.

cards.title: A good next step: Sound Therapy
cards.bodyMarkdown: Sound Therapy is a good place to begin because it works directly with the sound environment. It can make tinnitus feel less isolated, reduce the contrast with silence, and make the emotional and behavioral tools easier to use. If you are not sure where to go next, start there. You can always return to this section and update your Body / Mind / Life picture as your understanding changes.

modules.title: Sound Therapy
modules.purpose: Comfortable outside sound can make tinnitus less dominant without trying to erase it.
modules.overviewMarkdown:
Sound therapy means using comfortable outside sound to make tinnitus less dominant in your listening environment. The goal is not to blast tinnitus away or prove that you can ignore it. The goal is to give your ears and brain another sound to work with so tinnitus can gradually become less central.

This is often one of the most practical starting points in tinnitus management because it works directly with the sound experience. When sound therapy is used consistently and comfortably, it can help make the other skills in this app easier to use, including acceptance, mindfulness, distress tolerance, cognitive reframing, and sleep support.

cards.title: What you will learn in this section
cards.bodyMarkdown:
By the end of this section, you should understand why sound therapy can help the brain get used to tinnitus, how to choose sounds and devices that feel comfortable, and how to set the volume so tinnitus and sound therapy gently overlap.

The most important skill is finding the right volume level. Sound that is too quiet will not help much, while sound that completely covers tinnitus may become a form of avoidance. The useful range is where the sound therapy is clearly present, but tinnitus is not being pushed out of awareness entirely.

cards.title: Why sound therapy helps
cards.bodyMarkdown:
When tinnitus is the only noticeable sound, the brain may treat it as the most important thing in the room. Sound therapy changes that listening environment. By adding a neutral or soothing background sound, you reduce the contrast between silence and tinnitus.

Over time, this can help the brain treat tinnitus as a lower-priority signal. It may still be there, but it does not have to become the main focus or pull your attention as strongly. This process is gradual, and it works best when sound therapy is used patiently and consistently.

cards.title: What sound therapy is
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Sound therapy means adding soft, steady, or soothing sound to your environment. This might come from a fan, a sound machine, a phone app, a speaker, open-ear headphones, or hearing aids. The sound does not have to be special or complicated. It just needs to be comfortable and useful for you.

Think of sound therapy as an auditory backdrop. The outside sound gives your brain something else to hear, so tinnitus is not standing alone in silence. The aim is not to erase tinnitus in the moment, but to make the listening environment easier for your brain to handle.

cards.title: A restaurant example
cards.bodyMarkdown:
A simple way to understand sound therapy is to imagine sitting in a restaurant. Music, voices, and movement do not erase every small sound in the room, but they help those sounds blend into the background. The clink of silverware may still happen, but it usually does not demand your full attention.

Tinnitus can work in a similar way. When the room is completely quiet, tinnitus may feel isolated and intense. When gentle sound is added, tinnitus may still be present, but it has more competition and can begin to feel less intrusive.

cards.title: Why silence can make tinnitus feel louder
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Many people notice tinnitus most strongly in quiet. That does not necessarily mean tinnitus has become more dangerous or permanently louder. It may mean there is less outside sound competing for attention.

Sound therapy reduces the stark contrast between silence and tinnitus. That can lower the feeling that tinnitus is the only thing happening. For some people this helps with concentration, relaxation, evening routines, and sleep preparation. It also gives the brain repeated opportunities to learn that tinnitus can be present without needing an alarm response.

cards.title: Masking is not the same as sound therapy
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Many people use the word masking to mean any use of sound for tinnitus, but full masking and sound therapy are not the same thing. Full masking means turning sound up until tinnitus is completely covered. That can be useful for a short break or a high-distress moment, but it is not the main goal of sound therapy, as we discuss it here.

Sound therapy usually works best when it supports adaptation. That means the sound is comfortable and present, while tinnitus may still be partly audible. In that volume range, the brain can begin learning that tinnitus does not need to dominate or trigger constant monitoring.

cards.title: Short-term relief and long-term adaptation
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Full masking can feel good because it gives immediate relief from hearing tinnitus. The limitation is that the relief often stops when the masking sound stops. If the brain only learns that tinnitus must be hidden, tinnitus may feel more threatening when it returns.

A habituation-oriented sound therapy approach is different. It allows some awareness of tinnitus while adding a steady, supportive sound. This can help the brain learn that tinnitus is present but not urgent. That learning is usually slower than short-term masking, but it is often more useful for daily management.

cards.title: Finding the sound therapy sweet spot
cards.bodyMarkdown:
The sound therapy sweet spot is the range where you can hear both the sound therapy and your tinnitus. If the sound therapy is too quiet, it may not give your brain enough input to work with. If it is too loud and completely covers tinnitus, it may become more about escaping the sound than adapting to it.

The middle volume range is usually the most helpful. In that range, tinnitus is present, but it is not alone. Sound therapy becomes a calm companion to your listening environment rather than a battle to overpower tinnitus.

cards.title: The three volume zones
cards.bodyMarkdown:
The bottom zone is too quiet: the sound therapy is not audible enough to help. The top zone is too loud: the sound covers tinnitus completely, which may be useful briefly but is not the main long-term goal.

The middle zone is the target. You can hear the sound therapy and still have some awareness of tinnitus. That overlap gives the brain a chance to practice hearing tinnitus without treating it as the only sound that matters.

cards.title: Important terms
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Habituation means the brain adapts and becomes less reactive to a repeated stimulus. When habituation happens with tinnitus, you may still notice tinnitus if you listen for it, but it no longer creates the same stress or urgency.

Sound therapy means using gentle background sound to reduce the impact of tinnitus and support habituation. An external sound source is any device or method that delivers that sound, such as a fan, speaker, phone app, sound machine, hearing aids, or open-ear headphones.

cards.title: Choosing sounds
cards.bodyMarkdown:
There is no perfect sound for everyone. Some people like rain, ocean waves, crickets, fans, white noise, pink noise, gentle music, or other steady sounds. Some people like sounds that another person would find irritating. If it helps you and you can use it comfortably, it can be a good sound for you.

The best starting point is to try a few neutral or pleasant sounds and notice which ones feel comfortable or soothing. If a sound becomes annoying, you are not doing anything wrong. Try a different sound or change the setting.

cards.title: Choosing devices and sound sources
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Sound therapy can come from many places: a phone app, small speaker, sound machine, fan, open-ear headphones, bone-conduction headphones, or hearing aids. The right device depends on where you are, what you are doing, and what feels comfortable.

If you have hearing loss, hearing care deserves special attention. Hearing aids can act like a highly personalized form of sound therapy by restoring sounds the brain has been missing. For many people with hearing loss and tinnitus, addressing hearing directly is one of the most useful starting points.

cards.title: How to set the volume
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Start with the sound low. Slowly raise it until you can hear the sound therapy clearly. Then notice whether tinnitus is still partly present. If you cannot hear the sound therapy, it is too low. If tinnitus disappears completely, the sound may be louder than you need for everyday sound therapy.

Aim for a comfortable overlap. You should be aware of the support sound, and you may still notice tinnitus, but neither one should feel like it is taking over. The exact level may change from day to day, and that is okay.

cards.title: Using sound therapy during the day
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Sound therapy is often most useful during quiet tasks or times when tinnitus tends to grab your attention. You might use it while reading, doing work around the home, working at a desk, relaxing in the evening, or preparing for bed.

Consistency matters more than perfection. You do not need to analyze every minute. The goal is to give your brain repeated, comfortable exposure to a richer sound environment so tinnitus becomes less dominant over time.

cards.title: Using sound at night
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Many people notice tinnitus more at night because the environment is quieter and there are fewer distractions. Gentle sound at night can make the transition toward sleep feel less like a direct confrontation with tinnitus.

This does not mean sound therapy is a full sleep treatment. It is one supportive tool. If sleep is a persistent problem, or if there are signs of a sleep condition such as sleep apnea, that deserves proper evaluation. But for many people, a comfortable background sound can make bedtime feel less stark and less silent.

cards.title: How sound therapy supports the rest of the app
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Sound therapy is the main auditory tool in this app, but it works best as part of a bigger approach. Comfortable sound can make mindfulness easier, support distress tolerance, reduce the feeling of being trapped in silence, and give you a better environment for practicing acceptance and cognitive reframing.

That is why sound therapy appears in more than one place. It is not just a sound tool. It is a foundation that can support emotional regulation, attention flexibility, sleep routines, and everyday re-engagement.

cards.title: If sound feels sensitive
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Tinnitus and sound sensitivity often travel together. If ordinary sound feels sharp, uncomfortable, or threatening, it can be tempting to avoid sound as much as possible. That reaction makes sense, but living in a quieter and quieter world can sometimes keep the sound system on high alert.

For sound sensitivity, the same basic principle still applies: comfortable, controlled sound can help the system feel safer over time. The key is not to push into volume levels that are uncomfortable or painful. Start gently, stay below the point of sensitivity, and use sounds that feel enjoyable or neutral.

cards.title: Enjoyable music speaker practice
cards.bodyMarkdown:
One simple sound-sensitivity practice is to use enjoyable music on speakers for 10 to 15 minutes. Start with the volume all the way down. Slowly raise it until you begin to notice sensitivity, then lower it slightly below that point. Listen only if it feels comfortable.

The purpose is not to tolerate bothersome sound levels. The purpose is to give your brain and body a controlled sound experience where nothing bad happens. If the level changes from day to day, treat that information non-judgmentally.

cards.title: FAQ: How loud should sound therapy be?
cards.bodyMarkdown:
A useful starting point is just below the level where sound therapy would completely cover tinnitus. You want to hear the support sound and still have some awareness of tinnitus. That overlap is what makes it sound therapy rather than simply blocking tinnitus out.

There may be moments when fuller masking is useful for a short break. For daily management, though, the balanced volume level is usually the better target.

cards.title: FAQ: Does the type of sound matter?
cards.bodyMarkdown:
The type of sound matters mostly because you need to be able to use it comfortably. Nature sounds, steady noise, fan sounds, gentle music, crickets, or water sounds can all be reasonable options.

The best sound is not the one someone else calls perfect. It is the one that works for your ears, your environment, and your nervous system on that day.

cards.title: FAQ: Will sound therapy get rid of tinnitus?
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Sound therapy is not a promise that tinnitus will disappear. The more realistic goal is that tinnitus becomes less dominant, less threatening, and easier to live with.

Many people find that sound therapy helps reduce distress even when tinnitus is still present. That distinction is important: improvement can mean a better relationship with tinnitus, not only a change in the sound itself.

cards.title: FAQ: When should I use sound therapy?
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Use sound therapy when it helps you stay engaged with your life. That might mean quiet work, reading, relaxing, evening routines, or getting ready for sleep. The goal is not to become dependent on sound every moment of the day.

Use it as support. If you notice that you are using sound only to avoid ever hearing tinnitus, return to the sweet spot idea and the Acceptance and Change section.

cards.title: Main points to remember
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Sound therapy adds comfortable outside sound so tinnitus is not alone in silence. The sound should usually be audible but not overpowering. Consistency matters, and the sound you choose should be something you can use comfortably over time.

Sound therapy is also more powerful when it is combined with the rest of tinnitus management. It can support mindfulness, distress tolerance, sleep routines, cognitive reframing, and a more flexible relationship with tinnitus.

cards.title: Before you move on
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Before you leave this section, choose one small way you could use sound therapy this week. Keep it simple: one sound, one device, one situation. You can always adjust later.

It also helps to write a reminder to be patient with yourself. Sound therapy is a learning process. Some days will be easier than others, and needing to adjust the sound does not mean you are failing. It means you are listening and responding.

A simple way to understand sound therapy is to imagine sitting in a restaurant. Music, voices, and movement do not erase every small sound in the room, but they help those sounds blend into the background. The clink of silverware may still happen, but it usually does not demand your full attention.

Tinnitus can work in a similar way. When the room is completely quiet, tinnitus may feel isolated and intense. When gentle sound is added, tinnitus may still be present, but it has more competition and can begin to feel less intrusive.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Why silence can make tinnitus feel louder
audio.transcript:
Many people notice tinnitus most strongly in quiet. That does not necessarily mean tinnitus has become more dangerous or permanently louder. It may mean there is less outside sound competing for attention.

Sound therapy reduces the stark contrast between silence and tinnitus. That can lower the feeling that tinnitus is the only thing happening. For some people this helps with concentration, relaxation, evening routines, and sleep preparation. It also gives the brain repeated opportunities to learn that tinnitus can be present without needing an alarm response.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Masking is not the same as sound therapy
audio.transcript:
Many people use the word masking to mean any use of sound for tinnitus, but full masking and sound therapy are not the same thing. Full masking means turning sound up until tinnitus is completely covered. That can be useful for a short break or a high-distress moment, but it is not the main goal of sound therapy, as we discuss it here.

Sound therapy usually works best when it supports adaptation. That means the sound is comfortable and present, while tinnitus may still be partly audible. In that volume range, the brain can begin learning that tinnitus does not need to dominate or trigger constant monitoring.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Short-term relief and long-term adaptation
audio.transcript:
Full masking can feel good because it gives immediate relief from hearing tinnitus. The limitation is that the relief often stops when the masking sound stops. If the brain only learns that tinnitus must be hidden, tinnitus may feel more threatening when it returns.

A habituation-oriented sound therapy approach is different. It allows some awareness of tinnitus while adding a steady, supportive sound. This can help the brain learn that tinnitus is present but not urgent. That learning is usually slower than short-term masking, but it is often more useful for daily management.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Finding the sound therapy sweet spot
audio.transcript:
The sound therapy sweet spot is the range where you can hear both the sound therapy and your tinnitus. If the sound therapy is too quiet, it may not give your brain enough input to work with. If it is too loud and completely covers tinnitus, it may become more about escaping the sound than adapting to it.

The middle volume range is usually the most helpful. In that range, tinnitus is present, but it is not alone. Sound therapy becomes a calm companion to your listening environment rather than a battle to overpower tinnitus.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: The three volume zones
audio.transcript:
The bottom zone is too quiet: the sound therapy is not audible enough to help. The top zone is too loud: the sound covers tinnitus completely, which may be useful briefly but is not the main long-term goal.

The middle zone is the target. You can hear the sound therapy and still have some awareness of tinnitus. That overlap gives the brain a chance to practice hearing tinnitus without treating it as the only sound that matters.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Important terms
audio.transcript:
Habituation means the brain adapts and becomes less reactive to a repeated stimulus. When habituation happens with tinnitus, you may still notice tinnitus if you listen for it, but it no longer creates the same stress or urgency.

Sound therapy means using gentle background sound to reduce the impact of tinnitus and support habituation. An external sound source is any device or method that delivers that sound, such as a fan, speaker, phone app, sound machine, hearing aids, or open-ear headphones.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Choosing sounds
audio.transcript:
There is no perfect sound for everyone. Some people like rain, ocean waves, crickets, fans, white noise, pink noise, gentle music, or other steady sounds. Some people like sounds that another person would find irritating. If it helps you and you can use it comfortably, it can be a good sound for you.

The best starting point is to try a few neutral or pleasant sounds and notice which ones feel comfortable or soothing. If a sound becomes annoying, you are not doing anything wrong. Try a different sound or change the setting.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Choosing devices and sound sources
audio.transcript:
Sound therapy can come from many places: a phone app, small speaker, sound machine, fan, open-ear headphones, bone-conduction headphones, or hearing aids. The right device depends on where you are, what you are doing, and what feels comfortable.

If you have hearing loss, hearing care deserves special attention. Hearing aids can act like a highly personalized form of sound therapy by restoring sounds the brain has been missing. For many people with hearing loss and tinnitus, addressing hearing directly is one of the most useful starting points.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: How to set the volume
audio.transcript:
Start with the sound low. Slowly raise it until you can hear the sound therapy clearly. Then notice whether tinnitus is still partly present. If you cannot hear the sound therapy, it is too low. If tinnitus disappears completely, the sound may be louder than you need for everyday sound therapy.

Aim for a comfortable overlap. You should be aware of the support sound, and you may still notice tinnitus, but neither one should feel like it is taking over. The exact level may change from day to day, and that is okay.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Using sound therapy during the day
audio.transcript:
Sound therapy is often most useful during quiet tasks or times when tinnitus tends to grab your attention. You might use it while reading, doing work around the home, working at a desk, relaxing in the evening, or preparing for bed.

Consistency matters more than perfection. You do not need to analyze every minute. The goal is to give your brain repeated, comfortable exposure to a richer sound environment so tinnitus becomes less dominant over time.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Using sound at night
audio.transcript:
Many people notice tinnitus more at night because the environment is quieter and there are fewer distractions. Gentle sound at night can make the transition toward sleep feel less like a direct confrontation with tinnitus.

This does not mean sound therapy is a full sleep treatment. It is one supportive tool. If sleep is a persistent problem, or if there are signs of a sleep condition such as sleep apnea, that deserves proper evaluation. But for many people, a comfortable background sound can make bedtime feel less stark and less silent.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: How sound therapy supports the rest of the app
audio.transcript:
Sound therapy is the main auditory tool in this app, but it works best as part of a bigger approach. Comfortable sound can make mindfulness easier, support distress tolerance, reduce the feeling of being trapped in silence, and give you a better environment for practicing acceptance and cognitive reframing.

That is why sound therapy appears in more than one place. It is not just a sound tool. It is a foundation that can support emotional regulation, attention flexibility, sleep routines, and everyday re-engagement.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: If sound feels sensitive
audio.transcript:
Tinnitus and sound sensitivity often travel together. If ordinary sound feels sharp, uncomfortable, or threatening, it can be tempting to avoid sound as much as possible. That reaction makes sense, but living in a quieter and quieter world can sometimes keep the sound system on high alert.

For sound sensitivity, the same basic principle still applies: comfortable, controlled sound can help the system feel safer over time. The key is not to push into volume levels that are uncomfortable or painful. Start gently, stay below the point of sensitivity, and use sounds that feel enjoyable or neutral.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Enjoyable music speaker practice
audio.transcript:
One simple sound-sensitivity practice is to use enjoyable music on speakers for 10 to 15 minutes. Start with the volume all the way down. Slowly raise it until you begin to notice sensitivity, then lower it slightly below that point. Listen only if it feels comfortable.

The purpose is not to tolerate bothersome sound levels. The purpose is to give your brain and body a controlled sound experience where nothing bad happens. If the level changes from day to day, treat that information non-judgmentally.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: FAQ: How loud should sound therapy be?
audio.transcript:
A useful starting point is just below the level where sound therapy would completely cover tinnitus. You want to hear the support sound and still have some awareness of tinnitus. That overlap is what makes it sound therapy rather than simply blocking tinnitus out.

There may be moments when fuller masking is useful for a short break. For daily management, though, the balanced volume level is usually the better target.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: FAQ: Does the type of sound matter?
audio.transcript:
The type of sound matters mostly because you need to be able to use it comfortably. Nature sounds, steady noise, fan sounds, gentle music, crickets, or water sounds can all be reasonable options.

The best sound is not the one someone else calls perfect. It is the one that works for your ears, your environment, and your nervous system on that day.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: FAQ: Will sound therapy get rid of tinnitus?
audio.transcript:
Sound therapy is not a promise that tinnitus will disappear. The more realistic goal is that tinnitus becomes less dominant, less threatening, and easier to live with.

Many people find that sound therapy helps reduce distress even when tinnitus is still present. That distinction is important: improvement can mean a better relationship with tinnitus, not only a change in the sound itself.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: FAQ: When should I use sound therapy?
audio.transcript:
Use sound therapy when it helps you stay engaged with your life. That might mean quiet work, reading, relaxing, evening routines, or getting ready for sleep. The goal is not to become dependent on sound every moment of the day.

Use it as support. If you notice that you are using sound only to avoid ever hearing tinnitus, return to the sweet spot idea and the Acceptance and Change section.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Main points to remember
audio.transcript:
Sound therapy adds comfortable outside sound so tinnitus is not alone in silence. The sound should usually be audible but not overpowering. Consistency matters, and the sound you choose should be something you can use comfortably over time.

Sound therapy is also more powerful when it is combined with the rest of tinnitus management. It can support mindfulness, distress tolerance, sleep routines, cognitive reframing, and a more flexible relationship with tinnitus.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Before you move on
audio.transcript:
Before you leave this section, choose one small way you could use sound therapy this week. Keep it simple: one sound, one device, one situation. You can always adjust later.

It also helps to write a reminder to be patient with yourself. Sound therapy is a learning process. Some days will be easier than others, and needing to adjust the sound does not mean you are failing. It means you are listening and responding.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Sound safety and when to seek help
audio.transcript:
Use comfortable sound. Do not push into painful volume. If sound sensitivity is severe, worsening, or interfering with daily life, professional guidance can help. If you have hearing loss, sudden hearing changes, one-sided symptoms, pulsatile tinnitus, dizziness, neurological symptoms, or other medical concerns, consider appropriate hearing healthcare or medical evaluation.

This app teaches sound therapy as an educational self-management tool. It does not replace audiology, ENT, mental health care, sleep medicine, or emergency care when those are needed.

modules.title: Acceptance and Change
modules.purpose: Acceptance and change can work together: you notice what is here and choose useful next steps.
modules.overviewMarkdown:
When tinnitus feels difficult, it is natural to want it gone. That reaction makes sense. The problem is that tinnitus does not always respond to force, and the harder you fight to make it disappear in a single moment, the more your attention and energy can become wrapped around it.

Acceptance does not mean giving up. In this section, acceptance means acknowledging what is happening right now so you can use your energy more wisely. Change means taking practical steps that reduce distress, support daily life, and help you stay connected to what matters.

cards.title: What you will learn
cards.bodyMarkdown: By the end of this section, you should be able to tell the difference between acceptance and giving up, recognize how avoidance can make tinnitus more frustrating, describe how acceptance and change can happen at the same time, and practice at least one acceptance-based exercise for tinnitus-related stress.

cards.title: Pause and reflect: what happened last time?
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Think about a recent moment when tinnitus made you angry, upset, or tense. What did you do to handle that feeling? Did your response lower the stress, or did it keep the struggle going?

Now ask one small question: if I had accepted that tinnitus was present in that moment, stoping the fight against it without liking it or approving of it, what might have felt different?

cards.title: Acceptance means noticing what is here
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Acceptance means allowing yourself to notice that tinnitus is present without spending all your energy trying to erase it. It does not mean you like tinnitus. It does not mean you want it to stay. It does not mean you believe nothing can improve.

It means you are starting from reality: tinnitus is here right now, and the next useful step probably will not come from arguing with that fact.

cards.title: Change means acting where you have influence
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Change means taking active steps to improve your life and reduce distress. That might mean using sound therapy, asking for support, practicing mindfulness, communicating a need, or returning to an activity tinnitus has pushed aside.

Change does not have to mean forcing tinnitus to disappear. It can mean making today more workable, your environment more supportive, and your reactions less controlled by the sound.

cards.title: Acceptance is not resignation
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Many people hear the word acceptance and think it means throwing in the towel. That is not what we mean here.

Resignation says, “Nothing can change, so why try?” Acceptance says, “This is the situation I am in right now, and I can still choose the next useful step.” Acceptance is active. It helps you stop fighting the impossible in this moment so you can put effort into something that may actually help.

cards.title: Why trying only to eliminate tinnitus can backfire
cards.bodyMarkdown:
At the beginning, many people put all their energy into making tinnitus vanish. They may avoid quiet places, stop doing things they enjoy, search constantly for cures, or feel crushed whenever a treatment does not work right away.

Those reactions are understandable. But when your whole life becomes organized around eliminating tinnitus, tinnitus can become even more central. The struggle itself starts taking up the space that your routines, relationships, hobbies, and rest used to occupy.

cards.title: Avoidance can make life smaller
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Avoidance can bring short-term relief. Masking tinnitus fully, leaving a quiet room, canceling plans, or checking the internet again may feel like it lowers distress for a moment. The problem is that avoidance can also teach the brain that tinnitus is something you cannot face.

Over time, the world may get smaller. Acceptance helps reverse that pattern by asking, “What can I allow for this moment, and what useful action can I take anyway?”

cards.title: Sound therapy shows acceptance and change together
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Sound therapy is a good example of acceptance and change working together. If you use sound only to cover tinnitus completely all day, the purpose becomes escape. That may help briefly, but it can also keep the brain from learning that tinnitus is safe enough to tune out.

When sound therapy is set in the middle volume range, where you can hear the support sound and may still notice tinnitus, you are accepting enough of the sound for the brain to learn while still changing the environment to make it easier to tolerate.

cards.title: The Yes AND mindset
cards.bodyMarkdown:
The Yes AND mindset comes from the idea that two truths can exist at the same time. You can acknowledge tinnitus honestly and still take a useful next step.

For example: “Yes, my tinnitus is tough today, and I can use a gentle background sound while I get ready.” Or, “Yes, I wish this were different, and I can still go to dinner with friends.” The first half is acceptance. The second half is change.

cards.title: Two truths can sit next to each other
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Without this kind of both-and thinking, tinnitus can push you toward all-or-nothing choices: either I fix this completely, or my life is ruined. That trap is exhausting.

A more balanced view says: tinnitus can be present, and I can still take care of myself. I can dislike this sound, and I can still choose something meaningful. I can want improvement, and I can stop demanding that everything change before I live my life.

cards.title: The tug-of-war with tinnitus
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Imagine tinnitus on the other side of a rope in a tug of war. You pull harder and harder, trying to win. But the more you pull, the more tired and stuck you become.

Pulling the rope might look like masking tinnitus every moment, avoiding quiet places, arguing with the sound in your mind, or searching for answers long after the search has stopped helping. The question is not whether those reactions make sense. They do, and are reasonable things to do at first. The question is whether staying in the tug-of-war is giving you your life back.

cards.title: What would dropping the rope mean?
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Dropping the rope does not mean tinnitus wins. It does not mean you like tinnitus or accept that nothing can improve. It means you stop spending this moment on a fight that is not helping.

When you drop the rope, even briefly, you may have more energy for something else: using a coping tool, changing the room, resting, connecting with someone, or returning to an activity that matters.

cards.title: Important term: acceptance
cards.bodyMarkdown: Acceptance means embracing the present experience without spending all your energy suppressing it, fighting it, or denying it. It acknowledges what you cannot fully change right now and frees mental energy for more constructive actions.

cards.title: Important term: change
cards.bodyMarkdown: Change means taking active steps to enhance your well-being. That may include coping tools, goals, problem-solving, sound therapy, communication, or daily routines. Change focuses on what can improve, even when tinnitus is still present.

cards.title: Important term: dialectical thinking
cards.bodyMarkdown: Dialectical thinking means holding two truths at the same time. In tinnitus management, that might sound like: “Yes, I have tinnitus, and yes, I can still live a fulfilling life.” This reduces all-or-nothing thinking and supports balanced decisions.

cards.title: Important term: experiential avoidance
cards.bodyMarkdown: Experiential avoidance means trying to escape uncomfortable thoughts, feelings, sensations, or situations in ways that bring short-term relief but may increase distress over time. With tinnitus, avoidance can sometimes make life smaller and tinnitus more powerful.

cards.title: Step one: notice the fight
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Taking acceptance and change into real life begins with noticing when you are locked in battle. Are you telling yourself, “I will only be okay when this goes away”? Are you organizing the day around avoiding tinnitus?

You do not need to judge yourself for that reaction. The goal is to recognize the pattern early enough to choose something different.

cards.title: Step two: choose one useful action
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Once you notice the fight, ask what action would actually support you. That might be using sound therapy, taking one breath, asking for help, stepping away from an internet search, or rejoining something you care about.

This is where Yes AND becomes practical: “Yes, this is hard, and I can still do one thing that helps.”

cards.title: Reconnecting with what matters
cards.bodyMarkdown:
When tinnitus feels overwhelming, it can shrink your world. You may avoid hobbies, social opportunities, music, work tasks, quiet rooms, or routines that used to matter.

The values-driven action plan asks you to name one meaningful activity tinnitus has affected and choose one small step back toward it. You do not need to solve everything first. Re-engagement can begin with one realistic action.

cards.title: Why this mindset supports the rest of the app
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Acceptance and change are woven through the rest of tinnitus management. Sound therapy works better when it is not just escape. Mindfulness becomes more approachable when you are not using it as a test of silence. Cognitive reframing is easier when you can pause long enough to question a thought.

By accepting what you cannot instantly fix, you free energy for the parts of life you can influence: routines, stress, sleep, communication, attention, and meaningful activity.

cards.title: FAQ: Is acceptance the same as doing nothing?
cards.bodyMarkdown: No. Acceptance is not passive. It means you acknowledge what you cannot fully control in this moment and shift attention toward what you can do. That might mean using sound therapy, practicing a skill, asking for support, or choosing an activity that matters.

cards.title: FAQ: If I stop trying to fix tinnitus, won’t it get worse?
cards.bodyMarkdown: Usually, constant fixing and checking can make tinnitus feel bigger because it keeps the sound at the center of attention. Acceptance does not mean you stop caring. It means you stop letting tinnitus consume every moment while you continue using tools that support you.

cards.title: FAQ: Does acceptance mean I am stuck with tinnitus forever?
cards.bodyMarkdown: No. Acceptance does not predict the future. It means your life does not have to stay on hold until tinnitus changes. You can stay open to new treatments or strategies while still taking care of your life today.

cards.title: FAQ: How can I accept tinnitus when it feels overwhelming?
cards.bodyMarkdown: Start small. Acceptance may begin with one breath, one moment of noticing, or one choice not to react immediately. If the moment is too intense, use a distress tolerance skill first, then come back to acceptance when your mind has more room.

cards.title: Practice: Yes AND
cards.bodyMarkdown:
In this exercise, write three honest frustrations about tinnitus. For each one, begin with “Yes,” and name the frustration without softening it. Then add “AND,” followed by one action you can take.

For example: “Yes, tinnitus is louder at night, and I can use the relaxing rain sound I like while I wind down.” Notice how the sentence holds both acceptance and change.

cards.title: Practice: Reconnection with What Matters
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Choose one activity, routine, relationship, or value that tinnitus has affected. Then list small steps that could help you move toward it again.

The point is not to force yourself back all at once. It is to find the lowest-hanging fruit: one concrete step this week that reconnects you with something meaningful.

cards.title: Main points
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Acceptance does not mean you are okay with tinnitus. It means you stop spending all your energy on a fight you cannot win by force.

Change focuses on what you can influence: your sound environment, habits, attention, communication, self-talk, and daily choices. Yes AND is a simple way to combine acceptance and action. Reducing avoidance can lower stress and free energy for meaningful life.

cards.title: Before you move on
cards.bodyMarkdown:
Before you leave this section, write down one small way you can use acceptance as a starting point for change. You might also write a reminder to be patient with yourself as you practice.

This is not a skill you master all at once. It is something you return to each time tinnitus starts pulling you back into the fight.

For example: “Yes, my tinnitus is tough today, and I can use a gentle background sound while I get ready.” Or, “Yes, I wish this were different, and I can still go to dinner with friends.” The first half is acceptance. The second half is change.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Two truths can sit next to each other
audio.transcript:
Without this kind of both-and thinking, tinnitus can push you toward all-or-nothing choices: either I fix this completely, or my life is ruined. That trap is exhausting.

A more balanced view says: tinnitus can be present, and I can still take care of myself. I can dislike this sound, and I can still choose something meaningful. I can want improvement, and I can stop demanding that everything change before I live my life.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: The tug-of-war with tinnitus
audio.transcript:
Imagine tinnitus on the other side of a rope in a tug of war. You pull harder and harder, trying to win. But the more you pull, the more tired and stuck you become.

Pulling the rope might look like masking tinnitus every moment, avoiding quiet places, arguing with the sound in your mind, or searching for answers long after the search has stopped helping. The question is not whether those reactions make sense. They do, and are reasonable things to do at first. The question is whether staying in the tug-of-war is giving you your life back.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: What would dropping the rope mean?
audio.transcript:
Dropping the rope does not mean tinnitus wins. It does not mean you like tinnitus or accept that nothing can improve. It means you stop spending this moment on a fight that is not helping.

When you drop the rope, even briefly, you may have more energy for something else: using a coping tool, changing the room, resting, connecting with someone, or returning to an activity that matters.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Important term: acceptance
audio.transcript: Acceptance means embracing the present experience without spending all your energy suppressing it, fighting it, or denying it. It acknowledges what you cannot fully change right now and frees mental energy for more constructive actions.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Important term: change
audio.transcript: Change means taking active steps to enhance your well-being. That may include coping tools, goals, problem-solving, sound therapy, communication, or daily routines. Change focuses on what can improve, even when tinnitus is still present.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Important term: dialectical thinking
audio.transcript: Dialectical thinking means holding two truths at the same time. In tinnitus management, that might sound like: “Yes, I have tinnitus, and yes, I can still live a fulfilling life.” This reduces all-or-nothing thinking and supports balanced decisions.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Important term: experiential avoidance
audio.transcript: Experiential avoidance means trying to escape uncomfortable thoughts, feelings, sensations, or situations in ways that bring short-term relief but may increase distress over time. With tinnitus, avoidance can sometimes make life smaller and tinnitus more powerful.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Step one: notice the fight
audio.transcript:
Taking acceptance and change into real life begins with noticing when you are locked in battle. Are you telling yourself, “I will only be okay when this goes away”? Are you organizing the day around avoiding tinnitus?

You do not need to judge yourself for that reaction. The goal is to recognize the pattern early enough to choose something different.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Step two: choose one useful action
audio.transcript:
Once you notice the fight, ask what action would actually support you. That might be using sound therapy, taking one breath, asking for help, stepping away from an internet search, or rejoining something you care about.

This is where Yes AND becomes practical: “Yes, this is hard, and I can still do one thing that helps.”
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Reconnecting with what matters
audio.transcript:
When tinnitus feels overwhelming, it can shrink your world. You may avoid hobbies, social opportunities, music, work tasks, quiet rooms, or routines that used to matter.

The values-driven action plan asks you to name one meaningful activity tinnitus has affected and choose one small step back toward it. You do not need to solve everything first. Re-engagement can begin with one realistic action.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Why this mindset supports the rest of the app
audio.transcript:
Acceptance and change are woven through the rest of tinnitus management. Sound therapy works better when it is not just escape. Mindfulness becomes more approachable when you are not using it as a test of silence. Cognitive reframing is easier when you can pause long enough to question a thought.

By accepting what you cannot instantly fix, you free energy for the parts of life you can influence: routines, stress, sleep, communication, attention, and meaningful activity.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: FAQ: Is acceptance the same as doing nothing?
audio.transcript: No. Acceptance is not passive. It means you acknowledge what you cannot fully control in this moment and shift attention toward what you can do. That might mean using sound therapy, practicing a skill, asking for support, or choosing an activity that matters.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: FAQ: If I stop trying to fix tinnitus, won’t it get worse?
audio.transcript: Usually, constant fixing and checking can make tinnitus feel bigger because it keeps the sound at the center of attention. Acceptance does not mean you stop caring. It means you stop letting tinnitus consume every moment while you continue using tools that support you.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: FAQ: Does acceptance mean I am stuck with tinnitus forever?
audio.transcript: No. Acceptance does not predict the future. It means your life does not have to stay on hold until tinnitus changes. You can stay open to new treatments or strategies while still taking care of your life today.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: FAQ: How can I accept tinnitus when it feels overwhelming?
audio.transcript: Start small. Acceptance may begin with one breath, one moment of noticing, or one choice not to react immediately. If the moment is too intense, use a distress tolerance skill first, then come back to acceptance when your mind has more room.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Practice: Yes AND

In this exercise, write three honest frustrations about tinnitus. For each one, begin with “Yes,” and name the frustration without softening it. Then add “AND,” followed by one action you can take.

For example: “Yes, tinnitus is louder at night, and I can use the relaxing rain sound I like while I wind down.” Notice how the sentence holds both acceptance and change.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Practice: Reconnection with What Matters
audio.transcript:
Choose one activity, routine, relationship, or value that tinnitus has affected. Then list small steps that could help you move toward it again.

The point is not to force yourself back all at once. It is to find the lowest-hanging fruit: one concrete step this week that reconnects you with something meaningful.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Main points
audio.transcript:
Acceptance does not mean you are okay with tinnitus. It means you stop spending all your energy on a fight you cannot win by force.

Change focuses on what you can influence: your sound environment, habits, attention, communication, self-talk, and daily choices. Yes AND is a simple way to combine acceptance and action. Reducing avoidance can lower stress and free energy for meaningful life.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Before you move on
audio.transcript:
Before you leave this section, write down one small way you can use acceptance as a starting point for change. You might also write a reminder to be patient with yourself as you practice.

This is not a skill you master all at once. It is something you return to each time tinnitus starts pulling you back into the fight.

modules.title: Mindfulness
modules.purpose: Mindfulness is attention flexibility, not forced silence or forced relaxation.
modules.overviewMarkdown: Mindfulness means learning to notice what is happening right now without immediately fighting it, avoiding it, or judging it. For tinnitus, this does not mean liking the ringing or pretending it is pleasant. It means practicing the ability to notice tinnitus as one part of the moment, alongside your breath, body, thoughts, emotions, and the sounds around you.

cards.title: What you will practice in this section
cards.bodyMarkdown: In this section, you will learn what mindfulness is, how it differs from simple relaxation, and why it can be useful when tinnitus feels intrusive. You will practice noticing tinnitus without panic or avoidance, using present-moment awareness to interrupt thought spirals, and combining mindfulness with sound therapy, acceptance, and cognitive tools.

cards.title: What mindfulness means for tinnitus
cards.bodyMarkdown: Mindfulness is the practice of being fully present with your experiences, including thoughts, feelings, sensations, and sounds, without trying to push away discomfort or cling tightly to comfort. With tinnitus, this means gently noticing the ringing, buzzing, or hissing while also noticing the rest of the room, the body, the breath, and the activity you are doing. The skill is not to force tinnitus away. The skill is to widen attention so tinnitus is no longer the only thing your mind is holding.

cards.title: You do not have to like the ringing
cards.bodyMarkdown: A key idea in this section is that you do not have to like tinnitus for mindfulness to help. You are not trying to convince yourself that the sound is pleasant. You are practicing a less combative way of noticing it. When the mind stops treating tinnitus as an emergency every time it appears, the sound can begin to lose some of its emotional force.

cards.title: Mindfulness is not forced silence
cards.bodyMarkdown: Many people assume mindfulness means sitting silently for a long time and focusing on tinnitus. That misunderstanding can make mindfulness feel impossible. In this app, mindfulness is much broader. It can be one breath before you check your phone, a minute of noticing sounds during a walk, or a short pause while holding a warm drink. Silence is not required. Everyday sounds can become anchors for awareness.

cards.title: Mindfulness is not the same as relaxation
cards.bodyMarkdown: Mindfulness and relaxation often overlap, but they are not the same thing. Relaxation focuses on feeling calmer. Mindfulness focuses on noticing what is here with more steadiness and less judgment. Sometimes mindfulness will help you feel relaxed. Other times, it simply helps you notice stress, tinnitus, or frustration without reacting as quickly.

cards.title: Neutral observation and non-judgment
cards.bodyMarkdown: When tinnitus appears, the mind may quickly label it as awful, unbearable, or a sign that the day is ruined. Mindfulness gives you a different option: notice the sound and notice the reaction to the sound. You might silently label it, “ringing,” “thought,” or “frustration.” This does not erase tinnitus, but it creates a small pause between the sound and the reaction.

cards.title: Why non-judgment lowers reactivity
cards.bodyMarkdown: Tinnitus often becomes more distressing when the sound is paired with alarm, fear, self-blame, or catastrophic thoughts. Mindfulness-based approaches help by lowering emotional reactivity. Instead of automatically moving from “I hear tinnitus” to “I can’t stand this,” you practice noticing the sound, taking a breath, and letting the moment be larger than the tinnitus alone.

cards.title: Mindfulness can work with sound therapy
cards.bodyMarkdown: Sound therapy can make mindfulness more accessible. Gentle background sound gives your attention something neutral to notice, especially when silence makes tinnitus feel too sharp. Mindfulness then helps you use sound therapy without making it another form of panic or avoidance. Together, they support the same goal: helping tinnitus become less dominant in your awareness.

cards.title: Mindfulness supports acceptance
cards.bodyMarkdown: The acceptance section focused on dropping the struggle long enough to choose a useful next step. Mindfulness is how you practice that in real time. When you become aware of tinnitus, you can notice it, feel the urge to fight it, and choose where your attention goes next. This is not passive. It is active training in how you respond.

cards.title: Mini-practice: 3-2-1 senses
cards.bodyMarkdown: The 3-2-1 senses practice is a simple way to widen attention. Look around and name three things you can see. Then identify two sounds or auditory sensations you can notice. Finally, notice one physical sensation, such as your feet on the floor or clothing against your skin. Pause for a moment afterward and ask whether your awareness or mood shifted.

cards.title: Important terms
cards.bodyMarkdown: Mindfulness means paying attention, on purpose, to the present moment without judging what you notice as good or bad. Present-moment awareness means focusing on right now instead of replaying past difficult moments or jumping into future what-ifs. Non-judgment means approaching the experience with openness rather than immediately labeling it awful, unbearable, or your fault.

cards.title: Putting mindfulness into daily life
cards.bodyMarkdown: Mindfulness does not need to be saved for a special meditation session. You can practice it in small moments: before checking your phone, while sitting down, while walking, or when tinnitus first grabs your attention. If tinnitus appears, acknowledge it gently: “I hear that ringing.” Then expand attention to the body, the room, the breath, or the activity in front of you.

cards.title: Responding instead of reacting
cards.bodyMarkdown: A mindful pause gives you a moment to respond rather than react. That pause may be one breath, one label, or one shift of attention. The goal is not to make tinnitus disappear in that moment. The goal is to keep the sound from automatically deciding your mood, your behavior, or the next hour of your day.

cards.title: How mindfulness connects to the bigger picture
cards.bodyMarkdown: Mindfulness, similar to sound therapy, supports many of the other tools in this app. It strengthens acceptance by helping you observe tinnitus without immediate resistance. It supports sound therapy by helping you stay flexible whether background sound is present or not. It supports distress tolerance by giving you a pause button in difficult moments, and it supports cognitive reframing by helping you see thoughts as events in the mind rather than facts that must be obeyed.

cards.title: FAQ: Will mindfulness make me focus on tinnitus more?
cards.bodyMarkdown: At first, mindfulness may make you more aware of tinnitus because you are practicing noticing. That does not mean you are doing it wrong. The goal is to notice tinnitus alongside other experiences, not to stare at it mentally. With practice, awareness becomes broader and tinnitus tends to have less control over the whole moment.

cards.title: FAQ: Do I need silence?
cards.bodyMarkdown: No. Mindfulness can happen with traffic, fans, appliances, conversation, music, or sound therapy in the background. Everyday sound can help anchor attention. Tinnitus can be included in awareness without becoming the only sound that matters.

cards.title: FAQ: Is mindfulness relaxation?
cards.bodyMarkdown: Mindfulness and relaxation can overlap, but mindfulness is broader. You may feel calmer, but the main skill is learning to observe your experience and let go of harsh judgments. Sometimes you will practice mindfulness during a calm moment. Other times you will practice it while you are uncomfortable.

cards.title: FAQ: How long do I need to practice?
cards.bodyMarkdown: You do not need to meditate for long periods every day for mindfulness to matter. Short, frequent practices can build the same kind of skill. One breath, one minute of listening, or a brief 3-2-1 senses check-in can be enough to practice returning to the present moment.

cards.title: Exercise: Mindful Listening in Everyday Activity
cards.bodyMarkdown: Mindful Listening helps you practice broad awareness during something ordinary, such as washing dishes, walking, or sitting with a cup of tea. Begin the activity with a slow breath. Notice all the sounds you can hear: water, footsteps, traffic, birds, the hum of a room, and tinnitus if it is present. If you notice tinnitus, label it neutrally as “ringing,” then gently widen attention to the rest of the sound environment.

cards.title: Reflect after mindful listening
cards.bodyMarkdown: After a minute or two, pause and ask what changed. Did noticing other sounds shift your experience of tinnitus? Did your body or mood feel any different before and after the practice? There is no perfect answer. The point is to notice whether attention can widen, even briefly.

cards.title: Exercise: Sound Shifting Practice
cards.bodyMarkdown: Sound Shifting trains attention to move instead of getting locked onto one sound. Set a short timer for two to five minutes. Begin by gently noticing tinnitus for 15 to 20 seconds. Notice thoughts or feelings that arise, and label them simply as “thought” or “feeling.” Then shift attention to another sound, such as a fan, traffic, music, or your breathing. Continue moving back and forth in short intervals.

cards.title: Reflect after sound shifting
cards.bodyMarkdown: When the timer ends, ask how it felt to switch your attention on purpose. Did any emotions shift during the exercise? Did tinnitus feel different after attention moved away and returned? The goal is not to like tinnitus. The goal is to practice directing awareness rather than feeling stuck.

cards.title: Tips for sound shifting
cards.bodyMarkdown: Stay neutral when frustration appears. You can mentally note “frustration”, feel it, and try not to suppress it, and then continue. Keep the practice short at first; two or three rounds may be enough. As you become more comfortable, you can lengthen the timer or include more external sounds. You are building flexibility, not testing endurance.
cards.safetyNote: If practice feels overwhelming, shorten it or switch to grounding/distress tolerance.

cards.title: When mindfulness feels hard
cards.bodyMarkdown: Sometimes mindfulness will feel difficult, especially if tinnitus is loud or you are already distressed. That does not mean mindfulness is wrong for you. Make the practice smaller. Add comfortable sound. Use 3-2-1 senses instead of a longer exercise. If you feel overwhelmed, switch to distress tolerance tools first and come back to mindfulness later.
cards.safetyNote: If the user feels unsafe or in crisis, direct to safety information, not self-guided practice.

cards.title: Main points
cards.bodyMarkdown: Mindfulness helps you notice tinnitus without being ruled by it. It is not about erasing the sound, but changing the response to it. Short, regular practices can interrupt thought loops and support tools like sound therapy, acceptance, distress tolerance, and cognitive reframing. Being present can reduce fear when tinnitus changes or feels louder.

cards.title: Your mindfulness plan
cards.bodyMarkdown: Before you move on, choose one small way to include mindfulness in your routine. It might be one breath in the morning, a 3-2-1 senses check-in during the day, mindful listening during a daily task, or sound shifting when tinnitus feels sticky. Write a reminder to be patient with yourself. This skill grows through practice, not perfection.
