modules.title: Distress Tolerance
modules.purpose: These skills help you cool down intense tinnitus moments before choosing what to do next.
modules.overviewMarkdown: Distress tolerance is about what to do when tinnitus suddenly feels overwhelming. These skills are not meant to erase tinnitus or solve the whole problem in one move. Their purpose is to help you stay grounded, slow the spiral, and avoid reacting in a way that makes the moment harder. When tinnitus feels like it is pulling all of your attention, distress tolerance gives you a short-term bridge back to steadier thinking.

cards.title: What you will learn in this section
cards.bodyMarkdown: In this section, you will learn quick skills you can use when tinnitus feels intense. You will practice naming a fluctuation without assuming it is permanent, pausing before reacting, using your body to calm your nervous system, and choosing a response that supports your long-term well-being. The goal is not to never feel distress. The goal is to have a plan for what to do when distress shows up.

cards.title: Managing distress, not eliminating it
cards.bodyMarkdown: Distress tolerance focuses on managing emotional overwhelm in the short term. This matters for tinnitus because sudden changes in loudness, pitch, or intrusiveness can trigger panic, frustration, or a rush to do something drastic. In those moments, trying to force tinnitus away can make your attention narrow even more. Distress tolerance gives you a way to lower the intensity of the moment first, so you can decide what to do next with a clearer mind.

cards.title: Why panic makes tinnitus feel bigger
cards.bodyMarkdown: When you feel panicked about tinnitus, your brain pays closer attention to the sound. That extra attention can make tinnitus feel louder, sharper, or more threatening, even if the signal itself has not changed much. Distress tolerance interrupts this loop. A cold splash of water, a pause, a breath, or a short movement break gives your body another high-priority signal and gives your mind a chance to stop chasing the alarm.

cards.title: Use the word fluctuation, not spike
cards.bodyMarkdown: Language matters. The word spike can make a tinnitus change sound like a permanent emergency. The word fluctuation is more neutral. It reminds you that tinnitus can move up and down, shift in tone, and feel more or less intrusive depending on the day, the body, stress, sleep, attention, and environment. A difficult fluctuation can still be unpleasant, but naming it as a fluctuation helps reduce the automatic fear that it will stay this way forever.

cards.title: Distress tolerance is a short-term safety valve
cards.bodyMarkdown: Distress tolerance is different from longer-term tools like cognitive reframing or acceptance work. It does not try to change your core beliefs about tinnitus in the middle of a hard moment. It gives you a safety valve. Once your body and mind are less activated, then you can decide whether to use sound therapy, mindfulness, a thought record, a communication skill, or simply return to what you were doing.

cards.title: Important terms
cards.bodyMarkdown: A few terms will come up throughout this section. Distress tolerance means using skills to cope with intense emotions in the short term without making the situation worse. STOP is a quick pause-and-choose skill. TIPP is a group of body-based tools that can lower emotional intensity. Fluctuation is a neutral word for tinnitus changes, reminding you that a difficult sound moment is not automatically a permanent escalation.

cards.title: STOP: pause before reacting
cards.bodyMarkdown: The STOP skill gives you a way to insert a pause between noticing tinnitus distress and reacting to it. Stop. Take a step back. Observe what is happening in your body, thoughts, emotions, and urges. Then proceed mindfully by choosing a response that supports you. STOP is useful because tinnitus distress often grows when the first reaction takes over before you have a chance to think.

cards.title: TIPP: use the body to calm the mind
cards.bodyMarkdown: TIPP stands for Temperature, Intense movement, Paced breathing, and Paired muscle relaxation. These skills target the body’s stress response. When tinnitus distress pushes you into fight-or-flight mode, changing your physical state can help your mind come back online. The goal is not pain, exhaustion, or pushing your body too hard. The goal is safe, noticeable body-based regulation.
cards.safetyNote: Include exercise/temperature caveats.

cards.title: Practice before the tornado
cards.bodyMarkdown: Distress tolerance works best when you practice it before the hardest moment. Try STOP when you feel impatient in traffic. Practice paced breathing when you are mildly stressed. Notice what happens when you use cold water or a short movement break during a smaller frustration. Rehearsing these skills in ordinary moments makes them easier to find when tinnitus feels much more intense.

cards.title: From “fix this now” to “I can handle this moment”
cards.bodyMarkdown: A difficult tinnitus moment can create the feeling that something must be fixed immediately. Distress tolerance shifts the goal. Instead of demanding that tinnitus disappear right now, the goal becomes: I can handle this moment without making it worse. That shift matters. It lets you take the next useful step, whether that is sound therapy, a walk, a breathing practice, a call to someone supportive, or returning to an activity you care about.

cards.title: Mini-exercise: Grab an ice cube
cards.bodyMarkdown: Temperature can pull attention back into the body quickly. One simple version is holding a small ice cube for a short time and noticing the cold, the water, and the changing sensation. The goal is not pain. The goal is to give your nervous system a clear, safe, high-priority sensation so your mind has a moment to step out of the tinnitus spiral. If it becomes painful or unsafe, stop.
cards.safetyNote: Avoid pain and injury; stop if uncomfortable.

cards.title: Another sensory option: frozen orange grounding
cards.bodyMarkdown: Some people like a sensory grounding object that changes over time. A frozen orange can offer cold, texture, scent, and movement as it warms in your hand. You might notice frost, the peel, the citrus smell, or the way the surface softens. This can feel like a strange suggestion, but it gets your mind out of focusing on tinnitus. It is simply another way to give attention a safe, concrete place to land when tinnitus-related thoughts are spinning.
cards.safetyNote: App-native extension; not in printed workbook chapter.

cards.title: Exercise: Take a pause before reacting
cards.bodyMarkdown: When tinnitus fluctuates, it is easy to react immediately with frustration or panic. The STOP exercise helps you pause, assess what is happening, and choose a response that is more likely to help. Instead of being caught in the first automatic reaction, you give yourself a few seconds of space. That space can be enough to keep the moment from becoming larger than it needs to be.

cards.title: STOP steps
cards.bodyMarkdown: Start by mentally saying “Stop.” Then take a step back, either by changing your posture, taking a breath, or briefly moving to another space. Observe what is happening in your body and mind: emotions, thoughts, physical sensations, and urges. Then proceed mindfully. Ask, what response will help me in the long term? That might mean using a skill, continuing your activity, or choosing a small supportive action.

cards.title: Exercise: Use your body to calm your mind
cards.bodyMarkdown: When tinnitus distress is high, your body may act as if there is a threat. Your heart may race, your breathing may change, and your attention may lock onto the sound. TIPP skills work through the body. They do not argue with the mind. They change the physical state enough to help you feel more in control.

cards.title: TIPP: Temperature
cards.bodyMarkdown: Temperature means using a safe, noticeable temperature change to shift the body’s stress response. You might splash cool water on your face, hold a cool cloth, or briefly place your hands in cool water. The goal is not to cause pain through the cold. The goal is to create a strong enough sensation that your body and mind pause the alarm loop.
cards.safetyNote: Do not cause pain or unsafe exposure.

cards.title: TIPP: Intense movement, when appropriate
cards.bodyMarkdown: Intense movement means a brief burst of safe physical activity, such as marching in place, a few squats, jumping jacks, or a short walk. This is not a workout plan and it is not appropriate for every body or every situation. The idea is to burn off some stress energy and help the nervous system reset. Choose an option that is safe for you.
cards.safetyNote: Caveat for injury, medical issues, physical safety.

cards.title: TIPP: Paced breathing
cards.bodyMarkdown: Paced breathing slows the rhythm of the body. One simple pattern is to breathe in for about four seconds and breathe out for six to eight seconds. The longer exhale helps signal that your body does not need to stay in full alarm mode. You do not have to make the breath perfect. A few slower breaths can be enough to create a little space.

cards.title: TIPP: Paired muscle relaxation
cards.bodyMarkdown: Paired muscle relaxation means gently tensing and releasing a muscle group while pairing the release with a slower breath. You might raise your shoulders slightly, hold for a few seconds, and then let them drop as you exhale. The contrast between tension and release can help your body recognize that it does not need to stay braced.
cards.safetyNote: Do not force painful tension.

cards.title: How distress tolerance connects to the bigger picture
cards.bodyMarkdown: Distress tolerance sits between mindfulness and cognitive reframing. Mindfulness helps you notice what is happening. Distress tolerance helps when the intensity is too high to think clearly. Once the tornado slows down, cognitive reframing can help you look at the thoughts that made the moment feel even worse. This section also connects to acceptance: even if you cannot change tinnitus right now, you can change how you respond to the moment.

cards.title: FAQ: Will these skills make tinnitus quieter?
cards.bodyMarkdown: Distress tolerance skills do not directly change the tinnitus sound. Their job is to lower the emotional reaction that makes the sound feel unmanageable. When the body and mind are less alarmed, tinnitus may feel less dominating, even if the sound itself is still present.

cards.title: FAQ: What if I forget the skills when I am upset?
cards.bodyMarkdown: That is common. Skills are hardest to remember when distress is highest. Practice them during smaller frustrations so they become familiar. You can also keep a short reminder in My Plan or use the Distress Tolerance section as a quick reference. The goal is not perfect use. The goal is to build a response you can find more easily over time.

cards.title: FAQ: Is this just avoidance?
cards.bodyMarkdown: Distress tolerance is not meant to be a way of avoiding tinnitus forever. It is a short-term stabilizing step. Once you are calmer, you can return to the bigger tools: sound therapy, mindfulness, acceptance, cognitive reframing, communication, or sleep support. The purpose is to prevent a hard moment from becoming a bigger spiral.

cards.title: Main points
cards.bodyMarkdown: Distress tolerance helps you manage emotional overwhelm when tinnitus feels unmanageable. Skills like STOP and TIPP help you pause, settle the body, and respond more calmly. Using the word fluctuation can reduce catastrophic fear. Practicing these skills before crisis-level distress makes them more available when you need them. Distress tolerance works alongside mindfulness and cognitive reframing so you can handle difficult moments with more control.

cards.title: Your distress tolerance plan
cards.bodyMarkdown: Before you move on, choose one small way to bring distress tolerance into your routine. You might practice STOP once today, try paced breathing before bed, or write down which TIPP skill feels safest and most realistic for you. Then write one reminder to be patient with yourself. These skills become stronger through repetition, not perfection.

audio.transcript: Intense movement means a brief burst of safe physical activity, such as marching in place, a few squats, jumping jacks, or a short walk. This is not a workout plan and it is not appropriate for every body or every situation. The idea is to burn off some stress energy and help the nervous system reset. Choose an option that is safe for you.

audio.title: TIPP: Paced breathing
audio.transcript: Paced breathing slows the rhythm of the body. One simple pattern is to breathe in for about four seconds and breathe out for six to eight seconds. The longer exhale helps signal that your body does not need to stay in full alarm mode. You do not have to make the breath perfect. A few slower breaths can be enough to create a little space.

audio.title: TIPP: Paired muscle relaxation
audio.transcript: Paired muscle relaxation means gently tensing and releasing a muscle group while pairing the release with a slower breath. You might raise your shoulders slightly, hold for a few seconds, and then let them drop as you exhale. The contrast between tension and release can help your body recognize that it does not need to stay braced.

audio.title: How distress tolerance connects to the bigger picture
audio.transcript: Distress tolerance sits between mindfulness and cognitive reframing. Mindfulness helps you notice what is happening. Distress tolerance helps when the intensity is too high to think clearly. Once the tornado slows down, cognitive reframing can help you look at the thoughts that made the moment feel even worse. This section also connects to acceptance: even if you cannot change tinnitus right now, you can change how you respond to the moment.

audio.title: FAQ: What if I forget the skills when I am upset?

modules.title: Cognitive Reframing
modules.purpose: Reframing helps you slow down tinnitus-related thoughts and check whether they are accurate enough to guide your next action.
modules.overviewMarkdown: When tinnitus or sound sensitivity feels intense, the mind can jump quickly to conclusions: “This will ruin my whole day,” “I cannot handle any noise,” or “Nothing will ever get better.” Cognitive reframing helps you slow that process down. The goal is not to pretend tinnitus is easy or to force positive thinking. The goal is to notice the thought, check whether it is accurate, and build a more balanced response.

cards.title: What You’ll Learn in This Section
cards.bodyMarkdown: In this section, you will learn how to spot recurring tinnitus-related thought patterns, test distressing thoughts with evidence, and reframe them into statements that are more accurate and workable. You will also see how these skills can apply beyond tinnitus, including work stress, relationships, sleep concerns, and other moments when the mind jumps to worst-case conclusions.

cards.title: Why Tinnitus Thoughts Can Move So Fast
cards.bodyMarkdown: When tinnitus flares or sound sensitivity is triggered, your thoughts may move faster than your ability to evaluate them. A sound moment can become a story: “This is unbearable,” “I am powerless,” or “My day is over.” Those thoughts can increase anxiety or hopelessness, which can then lead to avoidance, checking, withdrawal, or frantic searching for relief. The sound may be real, but the story your mind adds can make the distress much larger.

cards.title: The Thoughts, Feelings, and Behaviors Loop
cards.bodyMarkdown: Cognitive behavioral therapy often describes a loop between what we think, how we feel, and what we do. With tinnitus, the loop might start with noticing the sound. That leads to a thought such as, “Today is going to be terrible.” That thought creates dread, and the dread may lead you to cancel plans, check tinnitus repeatedly, or search for a quick fix. Those behaviors then reinforce the next thought. Reframing gives you an off-ramp in that loop.

cards.title: Reality-Checking Your Mind
cards.bodyMarkdown: Think of cognitive restructuring as reality-checking your mind. First, identify the distressing thought. Next, ask whether the thought is fully accurate or whether it is leaving out evidence. Then create a more balanced statement. For example, “This ringing is awful, so my day is ruined” might become, “This moment is difficult, and I have had difficult tinnitus moments before without the entire day being lost.”

cards.title: Pause and Look Back on a Quick Reaction
cards.bodyMarkdown: A helpful way to understand reframing is to remember a time when you reacted quickly, then later saw the situation differently. Think of a recent tinnitus moment when your reaction was immediate. How did it feel then? How does it feel now? Were your fears still fully accurate later? This kind of reflection shows that the first thought is not always the most complete thought.

cards.title: Accurate Thinking, Not Forced Positivity
cards.bodyMarkdown: Cognitive restructuring is not about telling yourself that tinnitus is wonderful or that everything is fine. That would not be honest, and for many people it would not be believable. The goal is accuracy. “I will never have a good moment again” is usually too extreme. “Some days are hard, and I have also had moments where tinnitus bothered me less” is more balanced. That balance reduces the extra distress created by the thought.

cards.title: Why Reframing Helps Even If the Sound Is Still There
cards.bodyMarkdown: Cognitive reframing may not change the tinnitus itself. Instead, it changes the stress loop around the sound. When the mind treats tinnitus as danger, failure, or a permanent disaster, distress grows. When the mind learns to test those meanings, the emotional reaction often becomes more manageable. Tinnitus can still be unpleasant, but it does not have to control every next step.

cards.title: Using the Same Skill with Sound Sensitivity
cards.bodyMarkdown: The same pattern can happen with sound sensitivity. A sound may feel uncomfortable, and the mind may quickly jump to “I cannot handle any noise” or “I have to avoid everything.” Sometimes caution is appropriate, especially around painful or unsafe sound. But reframing helps you separate reasonable protection from a story that makes life smaller than it needs to be.
cards.safetyNote: Do not encourage painful sound exposure; keep sound sensitivity advice tied to comfort and professional support when needed.

cards.title: Example: A Loud Tinnitus Morning
cards.bodyMarkdown: A common thought is, “My tinnitus is loud this morning, so today will be terrible.” That thought feels like it makes sense in the moment, but it is not guaranteed. You may have had loud tinnitus before and still had a meaningful, productive, or even good day. A more balanced statement might be, “This morning is difficult, and I can use my tools while I see how the day unfolds.”

cards.title: Term: Cognitive Restructuring
cards.bodyMarkdown: Cognitive restructuring is a step-by-step way to identify and challenge negative thoughts. Rather than “think positive,” it asks you to think accurately, using real evidence from your own experience.

cards.title: Term: Distorted Thought
cards.bodyMarkdown: A distorted thought is an unhelpful or exaggerated belief. Examples include “I can’t cope with any noise,” “This will never improve,” or “Everyone thinks I am overreacting.” These thoughts can feel true before they have been checked.

cards.title: Term: Reframing
cards.bodyMarkdown: Reframing means shifting a rigid or negative view into a more balanced one. “This tinnitus ruins everything” might become, “This is unpleasant, and it does not have to decide everything I do today.”

cards.title: Term: Behavioral Experiment
cards.bodyMarkdown: A behavioral experiment is a small real-world test of a thought. If your thought is, “I cannot sit in a coffee shop,” a small experiment might be visiting briefly, using a sound strategy, and noticing what actually happens. The goal is to gather evidence, not to force yourself into distress.
cards.safetyNote: Do not frame as pushing through unsafe sound or severe distress.

cards.title: Start with Small Thought Moments
cards.bodyMarkdown: Cognitive reframing works best when it is practiced in real life. Start with a small moment: “I will never get through this meeting,” “This sound is too much,” or “I am failing at tinnitus management.” Write the thought down, check the facts, and create a more balanced statement. Over time, the skill becomes less like a worksheet and more like a mental pause you can use in the moment.

cards.title: You Will Miss Most Thoughts at First
cards.bodyMarkdown: At the beginning, you may miss most automatic thoughts until after the moment has passed. That is normal. The first goal is not to catch every thought. The goal is to notice one pattern that you would have missed before. If you catch one out of twenty, that is progress, because the pattern is becoming visible.

cards.title: The Cognitive Distortion Library
cards.bodyMarkdown: Cognitive distortions are common thinking shortcuts. They are not signs that you are doing something wrong; they are patterns to notice. Naming the pattern gives you a little distance from it. You do not need to pick the perfect label. If the label helps you pause and question the thought, it has done its job.

cards.title: All-or-Nothing Thinking
cards.bodyMarkdown: All-or-nothing thinking turns a complicated situation into two choices: perfect or ruined. With tinnitus, this might sound like, “If my tinnitus does not go away completely, my life will be ruined.” A more balanced view looks for the middle ground: life may be harder right now, and it can still contain useful, meaningful, or manageable moments.

cards.title: Overgeneralization
cards.bodyMarkdown: Overgeneralization takes one moment and stretches it too far. “My tinnitus was loud today, so it will be like this every day” is a prediction based on limited evidence. Reframing asks what else you know from experience: tinnitus often changes, and one day does not prove the future.

cards.title: Filtering
cards.bodyMarkdown: Filtering means the mind locks onto the distressing evidence and filters out everything else. You might dismiss a good day because today is harder. Reframing does not deny today’s difficulty; it asks you to include the fuller picture.

cards.title: Mind Reading
cards.bodyMarkdown: Mind reading happens when you assume you know what others think. With tinnitus, it may sound like, “People think I am overreacting.” Sometimes people may not understand, but that is different from knowing what they think. Reframing asks what evidence you actually have and whether communication could help.

cards.title: Minimizing
cards.bodyMarkdown: Minimizing downplays progress. If you used sound therapy, practiced breathing, went to dinner, or had a quieter hour, that matters. The improvement may not be perfect, but it is still evidence that your choices can influence the experience.

cards.title: Catastrophizing
cards.bodyMarkdown: Catastrophizing turns a hard moment into a disaster story. “My tinnitus will only get worse, and I will never handle it” may feel convincing when distress is high. Reframing asks whether the evidence truly proves that outcome, and what a more grounded next thought could be.

cards.title: Control Fallacies
cards.bodyMarkdown: Control fallacies make it feel like you have either total control or no control at all. Tinnitus management usually lives in the middle. You may not control every sound moment, but you can influence your sound environment, attention, routines, and response.

cards.title: Heaven’s Reward Fallacy
cards.bodyMarkdown: Heaven’s reward fallacy is the belief that suffering harder will eventually pay off by itself. Enduring tinnitus without using tools does not necessarily make it improve faster. A more useful question is, “What action actually supports me today?”

cards.title: Labeling
cards.bodyMarkdown: Labeling turns a struggle into an identity. “I am having a hard tinnitus day” is very different from “I am a failure.” Reframing helps separate the difficulty of the moment from your worth as a person.

cards.title: Personalization
cards.bodyMarkdown: Personalization puts all the blame on you, even when the situation is more complicated. You may wish you had done something differently in the past, but self-blame usually does not guide the next useful step. Reframing helps separate responsibility, regret, and self-attack.

cards.title: Exercise: Identifying and Naming Cognitive Distortions
cards.bodyMarkdown: When you notice a distressing tinnitus-related thought, write it down. Then choose the thinking pattern that seems closest. Ask what evidence supports the thought, what evidence contradicts it, and what a more balanced way to view the situation might be. You do not need the perfect label; you need enough distance to question the thought.

cards.title: Exercise: Evidence For-and-Against
cards.bodyMarkdown: Choose one negative belief about tinnitus or sound sensitivity. Write the evidence that seems to support it, then the evidence that does not support it. Use both sides to create a more balanced statement. This exercise works because it turns a loud thought into something testable.

cards.title: Testing a Thought in Real Life
cards.bodyMarkdown: Sometimes the next step is to test a thought gently. If you believe, “I cannot handle a social outing,” a small test might be attending for a limited time with a sound plan and an exit option. Afterward, you look at what actually happened. The purpose is not to prove yourself wrong by force; it is to gather real evidence in a manageable way.
cards.safetyNote: Do not use for unsafe sound exposure or severe distress without support.

cards.title: How Reframing Connects to the Bigger Picture
cards.bodyMarkdown: Cognitive reframing works best when it is connected to the other tools. If distress is very high, start with distress tolerance to cool the moment down. Mindfulness helps you notice the thought before reacting. Acceptance helps you stop fighting reality long enough to choose a useful step. Reframing then asks whether the thought guiding that step is accurate enough to trust.

cards.title: This Skill Can Spread Beyond Tinnitus
cards.bodyMarkdown: Many people first learn these patterns through tinnitus, then notice them elsewhere. The same catastrophizing that says tinnitus will ruin the day might also appear when your inbox is full, a relationship feels tense, or a project feels overwhelming. Once you recognize the pattern, you can use the same skill in more than one area of life.

cards.title: FAQ: Is Cognitive Restructuring Forced Positivity?
cards.bodyMarkdown: No. Forced positivity would ask you to say something cheerful that you do not believe. Cognitive restructuring asks whether the thought is accurate, complete, and useful. You still acknowledge discomfort, but you do not let worst-case assumptions become the only story.

cards.title: FAQ: How Do I Know If a Thought Is Distorted?
cards.bodyMarkdown: Look for extreme words like “always,” “never,” or “ruined.” Notice whether the thought predicts disaster without proof, ignores progress, or turns one moment into a conclusion about your whole future. If the thought feels urgent and absolute, it is worth checking.

cards.title: FAQ: Will Reframing Silence My Tinnitus?
cards.bodyMarkdown: Reframing does not silence tinnitus. It reduces the distress loop around tinnitus. The sound may still be present, but the meaning attached to the sound can become less threatening, which can make the experience easier to handle.

cards.title: FAQ: Do I Have to Do a Thought Record Every Time?
cards.bodyMarkdown: No. Thought records are training tools. At first, writing things down helps you learn the process. Later, you may be able to notice the pattern, check the evidence, and reframe the thought mentally. The written exercise is a way to build the skill.

cards.title: Main Points
cards.bodyMarkdown: Cognitive reframing helps you identify thoughts that make tinnitus distress larger. The goal is realistic thinking, not forced optimism. You can check evidence for and against a thought, name common distortion patterns, and build a more balanced response. With practice, this becomes a flexible skill that can help with tinnitus and other stressful parts of life.

cards.title: Your Cognitive Reframing Plan
cards.bodyMarkdown: Before you move on, choose one small way to practice cognitive reframing this week. You might write down one tinnitus-related thought each day, practice one Evidence For-and-Against exercise, or simply watch for one repeated pattern like catastrophizing. Add a reminder to be patient with yourself while the skill develops.

audio.transcript: Control fallacies make it feel like you have either total control or no control at all. Tinnitus management usually lives in the middle. You may not control every sound moment, but you can influence your sound environment, attention, routines, and response.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Heaven’s Reward Fallacy
audio.transcript: Heaven’s reward fallacy is the belief that suffering harder will eventually pay off by itself. Enduring tinnitus without using tools does not necessarily make it improve faster. A more useful question is, “What action actually supports me today?”
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Labeling
audio.transcript: Labeling turns a struggle into an identity. “I am having a hard tinnitus day” is very different from “I am a failure.” Reframing helps separate the difficulty of the moment from your worth as a person.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Personalization
audio.transcript: Personalization puts all the blame on you, even when the situation is more complicated. You may wish you had done something differently in the past, but self-blame usually does not guide the next useful step. Reframing helps separate responsibility, regret, and self-attack.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Exercise: Identifying and Naming Cognitive Distortions
audio.transcript: When you notice a distressing tinnitus-related thought, write it down. Then choose the thinking pattern that seems closest. Ask what evidence supports the thought, what evidence contradicts it, and what a more balanced way to view the situation might be. You do not need the perfect label; you need enough distance to question the thought.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Exercise: Evidence For-and-Against
audio.transcript: Choose one negative belief about tinnitus or sound sensitivity. Write the evidence that seems to support it, then the evidence that does not support it. Use both sides to create a more balanced statement. This exercise works because it turns a loud thought into something testable.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Testing a Thought in Real Life
audio.transcript: Sometimes the next step is to test a thought gently. If you believe, “I cannot handle a social outing,” a small test might be attending for a limited time with a sound plan and an exit option. Afterward, you look at what actually happened. The purpose is not to prove yourself wrong by force; it is to gather real evidence in a manageable way.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: How Reframing Connects to the Bigger Picture
audio.transcript: Cognitive reframing works best when it is connected to the other tools. If distress is very high, start with distress tolerance to cool the moment down. Mindfulness helps you notice the thought before reacting. Acceptance helps you stop fighting reality long enough to choose a useful step. Reframing then asks whether the thought guiding that step is accurate enough to trust.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: This Skill Can Spread Beyond Tinnitus
audio.transcript: Many people first learn these patterns through tinnitus, then notice them elsewhere. The same catastrophizing that says tinnitus will ruin the day might also appear when your inbox is full, a relationship feels tense, or a project feels overwhelming. Once you recognize the pattern, you can use the same skill in more than one area of life.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: FAQ: Is Cognitive Restructuring Forced Positivity?
audio.transcript: No. Forced positivity would ask you to say something cheerful that you do not believe. Cognitive restructuring asks whether the thought is accurate, complete, and useful. You still acknowledge discomfort, but you do not let worst-case assumptions become the only story.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: FAQ: How Do I Know If a Thought Is Distorted?
audio.transcript: Look for extreme words like “always,” “never,” or “ruined.” Notice whether the thought predicts disaster without proof, ignores progress, or turns one moment into a conclusion about your whole future. If the thought feels urgent and absolute, it is worth checking.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: FAQ: Will Reframing Silence My Tinnitus?
audio.transcript: Reframing does not silence tinnitus. It reduces the distress loop around tinnitus. The sound may still be present, but the meaning attached to the sound can become less threatening, which can make the experience easier to handle.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: FAQ: Do I Have to Do a Thought Record Every Time?
audio.transcript: No. Thought records are training tools. At first, writing things down helps you learn the process. Later, you may be able to notice the pattern, check the evidence, and reframe the thought mentally. The written exercise is a way to build the skill.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Main Points
audio.transcript: Cognitive reframing helps you identify thoughts that make tinnitus distress larger. The goal is realistic thinking, not forced optimism. You can check evidence for and against a thought, name common distortion patterns, and build a more balanced response. With practice, this becomes a flexible skill that can help with tinnitus and other stressful parts of life.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Your Cognitive Reframing Plan
audio.transcript: Before you move on, choose one small way to practice cognitive reframing this week. You might write down one tinnitus-related thought each day, practice one Evidence For-and-Against exercise, or simply watch for one repeated pattern like catastrophizing. Add a reminder to be patient with yourself while the skill develops.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: When Thought Work Is Not the First Step
audio.transcript: If distress is extremely high, cognitive reframing may not be the first tool to use. Start with a grounding or distress tolerance skill until your mind has enough space to think. If you feel unsafe, are in a mental health crisis, or feel unable to care for yourself, do not rely on this app. Seek immediate support through emergency services, crisis resources, or a qualified professional.

modules.title: Confidence and Communication
modules.purpose: This section helps you support yourself and communicate tinnitus-related needs more clearly.
modules.overviewMarkdown: Tinnitus can affect how you speak to yourself and how you communicate with the people around you. This section brings together two related skills: building a more supportive inner voice, and asking for what you need clearly and respectfully.

cards.title: Why these topics fit together
cards.bodyMarkdown: Self-compassion and validation are the internal side of support. Interpersonal effectiveness is the external side. One helps you stop adding shame or self-blame to tinnitus, and the other helps you explain your needs without withdrawing, over-apologizing, or feeling like your experience does not matter.

cards.title: What you will learn in this section
cards.bodyMarkdown: By the end of this section, you should be able to notice self-critical thoughts, respond to yourself with more patience, validate that your tinnitus distress is real, and make a clear request when your sound environment or communication needs matter. You do not need to master every skill at once. The goal is to find one or two responses that help you stay connected to yourself and to others.

cards.title: When tinnitus turns into self-criticism
cards.bodyMarkdown: When tinnitus fluctuates, many people quickly turn frustration inward. Thoughts like “I should be able to ignore this,” “Why am I so weak?” or “I should be coping better” can add another layer of distress on top of the sound itself. Self-compassion does not pretend tinnitus is easy. It helps you respond to a hard moment without attacking yourself for having it.

cards.title: Self-compassion is not giving up
cards.bodyMarkdown: Some people worry that being kind to themselves will make them passive. In practice, the opposite is often true. Harsh self-talk drains emotional energy. A more compassionate response gives you a steadier place to practice the tools you are learning: sound therapy, mindfulness, reframing, communication, and sleep support.

cards.title: The three parts of self-compassion
cards.bodyMarkdown: Self-compassion has three main parts. Self-kindness means responding to your own pain with warmth instead of harshness. Common humanity means remembering that many people struggle with tinnitus and other chronic symptoms, even if their experience is not exactly the same as yours. Mindful awareness means noticing distress without exaggerating it or pushing it away completely.

cards.title: Self-kindness: how would you respond to someone you care about?
cards.bodyMarkdown: A useful self-compassion question is: what would I say to someone I care about if they were having this same moment? Most people would not say, “You should be handling this better.” They would say something more patient, honest, and supportive. The goal is to offer yourself that same kind of response.

cards.title: Common humanity: you are not the only person struggling
cards.bodyMarkdown: Tinnitus can feel isolating because the sound is subjective. Other people don’t hear it, and they may not understand why it affects you so much. Common humanity does not erase the individual nature of tinnitus, but it reminds you that the distress, frustration, fear, and exhaustion are shared by many people. You are not failing because this is hard.

cards.title: Mindful awareness: notice without amplifying
cards.bodyMarkdown: Mindful awareness means noticing what is happening without immediately turning it into a larger story. You might say, “This is a difficult tinnitus moment,” rather than “I am never going to be okay.” That small change matters. It lets you acknowledge distress without letting the self-critical voice take over the whole situation.

cards.title: Validation: your reaction makes sense
cards.bodyMarkdown: Validation means recognizing that your emotional response is real and understandable. If tinnitus is intrusive, unpredictable, or affecting sleep, it makes sense that you may feel upset. Validation is not the same as saying nothing can improve. It simply starts from the truth: this is hard, and your reaction is not a personal weakness.

cards.title: A brief validation practice
cards.bodyMarkdown: The next time tinnitus changes or feels difficult to manage, try three short steps. First, notice the immediate reaction. Second, state one sentence that validates it: “Of course I feel upset; this sound is intrusive.” Third, add self-compassion: “I am not alone, and I can take this one step at a time.” Then notice whether the tension changes, even slightly.

cards.title: From self-blame to a supportive inner voice
cards.bodyMarkdown: Self-compassion does not require you to enjoy tinnitus or pretend you are fine. It asks you to stop adding blame to an already difficult experience. A supportive inner voice might sound like: “This is hard right now, and I can still use one tool.” That kind of response leaves more room for action than “I should be better at this.”

cards.title: Optional mini-practice: give tinnitus a nickname
cards.bodyMarkdown: Some people find it helpful to imagine tinnitus as a character rather than a threat. A name like “Buzz” or “Ringo” can add a little distance or humor. This is not meant to make tinnitus cute or harmless if it feels serious. It is simply a way to loosen the grip of fear and speak to the experience with less alarm.

cards.title: Important terms: self-compassion and validation
cards.bodyMarkdown: Self-compassion means treating yourself with kindness when you are having a hard time. Validation means recognizing that your emotional experience is real and understandable. Common humanity reminds you that many people struggle with similar feelings. The self-critical voice is the inner commentary that says you should be coping better, even when you are already doing something difficult.

cards.title: Putting self-compassion into practice
cards.bodyMarkdown: Self-compassion works best when it becomes small and repeatable. You might use a phrase before bed, after a difficult sound moment, or after catching a distorted thought. Try something honest, not overly positive: “This is difficult, and I am doing my best in a tough situation.” Over time, these small responses reduce the load of shame and make it easier to return to practical tools.

cards.title: How self-compassion connects to the other tools
cards.bodyMarkdown: Self-compassion supports the rest of tinnitus management. Mindfulness helps you notice difficult thoughts. Cognitive reframing helps you question them. Self-compassion helps you avoid attacking yourself for having them in the first place. That emotional cushion can make sound therapy, acceptance, and distress tolerance easier to keep using on hard days.

cards.title: FAQ: Won’t kindness make me less motivated?
cards.bodyMarkdown: Kindness is not laziness. Self-compassion can actually support motivation because it reduces the exhaustion of self-criticism. You are more likely to keep practicing when your inner voice is firm and supportive instead of punishing.

cards.title: FAQ: Is self-compassion just self-pity?
cards.bodyMarkdown: Self-pity tends to keep you stuck in the problem. Self-compassion acknowledges the problem while still making room for action. It says, “This is hard, and I can take care of myself while I figure out how to manage it.”

cards.title: FAQ: How do I validate myself when others dismiss tinnitus?
cards.bodyMarkdown: Other people may oversimplify tinnitus because they cannot hear what you hear or feel what you feel. Validation starts by reminding yourself that your distress is real. You can accept that your feelings make sense even if someone else does not fully understand them.

cards.title: FAQ: What if kind self-talk feels awkward?
cards.bodyMarkdown: That is normal. Many people are not used to speaking to themselves this way. Start with a phrase you might say to a friend. The goal is not to sound perfect; it is to practice a more helpful tone.

cards.title: Exercise: re-scripting a self-critical thought
cards.bodyMarkdown: This exercise helps you practice changing the tone of your inner dialogue. Start with one recent self-critical thought. Notice how it makes you feel. Then imagine that someone you care about said the same thing about themselves. Write the response you would offer them, and adjust it into a compassionate statement you could use for yourself.

cards.title: Main points for supporting yourself
cards.bodyMarkdown: Self-compassion reduces the extra distress that comes from blaming yourself. Validation reminds you that your reaction is real and understandable. Common humanity helps reduce isolation. A supportive inner voice does not remove tinnitus, but it can keep you more steady while you practice the tools that help.

cards.title: Why communication matters with tinnitus
cards.bodyMarkdown: Tinnitus is invisible, which means other people may not know what you are dealing with unless you explain it. Sound environments, background noise, hearing difficulty, and sound sensitivity can all affect communication. Interpersonal effectiveness helps you ask for what you need without withdrawing, over-apologizing, or waiting until frustration turns into conflict.

cards.title: Invisible symptoms can create misunderstanding
cards.bodyMarkdown: Because other people cannot hear your tinnitus, they may underestimate how much it affects you. Some may say, “I have ringing too,” without realizing your experience is different. Skillful communication gives you a way to explain the impact without needing to prove your suffering. It also helps prevent the isolation that can happen when you stay silent.

cards.title: Self-advocacy without guilt
cards.bodyMarkdown: Asking for a quieter table, a lower TV volume, or a short break does not make you difficult. It is a way to stay engaged while respecting your limits. The goal is not to control everyone around you. The goal is to communicate clearly enough that others understand what would help.

cards.title: DEAR MAN: a structure for clear requests
cards.bodyMarkdown: DEAR MAN is a DBT communication tool for making a request or saying no clearly. The first part, DEAR, helps you organize what you want to say: describe the situation, express how it affects you, assert what you need, and reinforce why the request helps. The second part, MAN, helps you stay focused, appear confident, and negotiate when needed.

cards.title: DEAR: describe, express, assert, reinforce
cards.bodyMarkdown: Start with the facts. Describe the situation in neutral terms: “The TV volume is making it hard for me to stay comfortable.” Then express how it affects you: “I feel overwhelmed when it stays this loud.” Next, assert the request clearly: “Could we lower it a little?” Finally, reinforce why it helps: “That would let me stay in the room and enjoy the evening with you.”

cards.title: MAN: stay mindful, appear confident, negotiate
cards.bodyMarkdown: After making the request, stay mindful of your goal. It is easy to get pulled into overexplaining, apologizing, or arguing. Appearing confident does not mean being aggressive; it means using a steady tone and clear words. Negotiating means staying open to workable solutions, such as moving seats, lowering volume, or taking a short break.

cards.title: Mini-practice: speak up in one sentence
cards.bodyMarkdown: Start small. Identify one request that could make a sound situation easier, such as “Could we lower the TV a little?” Practice saying it in one calm sentence. Then use it in a low-pressure moment and notice what happens. Even a short request can show that self-advocacy does not have to be a burden.

cards.title: Important terms: communication and self-respect
cards.bodyMarkdown: Interpersonal effectiveness means balancing your needs with the relationship in front of you. DEAR MAN helps you make a request clearly.

cards.title: Putting communication skills into practice
cards.bodyMarkdown: Think of these skills as bridges between tinnitus needs and daily life. Instead of quietly enduring a noisy room or snapping after you are already overwhelmed, you can make a clear, respectful request earlier. Start in low-pressure situations. Success builds confidence, and confidence makes it easier to stay connected rather than withdrawing.

cards.title: How communication connects to the bigger picture
cards.bodyMarkdown: Communication works best when it is paired with the other skills. Distress tolerance can steady your body before a hard conversation. Self-compassion can reduce guilt about asking for help. Sound therapy can make an environment easier to tolerate. Together, these tools help you stay involved in life instead of feeling forced into silence or isolation.

cards.title: FAQ: Will asking for quieter options make me seem needy?
cards.bodyMarkdown: A clear, polite request often feels better to others than silent frustration. You are not asking people to understand everything about tinnitus. You are asking for one reasonable adjustment that may help you stay present.

cards.title: FAQ: What if someone dismisses my tinnitus?
cards.bodyMarkdown: That can happen, and it can hurt. DEAR MAN helps you stay clear about what you need, but communicating and getting what we want are different.  There will be times where communicating well will not create the outcome we are hoping for.

cards.title: FAQ: Is DEAR MAN too structured for real life?
cards.bodyMarkdown: It may feel structured at first, but the point is not to recite the letters. The steps help you organize your message. Even using part of the skill can make a conversation clearer.

cards.title: FAQ: What if I feel guilty inconveniencing others?
cards.bodyMarkdown: Guilt is common, especially when tinnitus is new or invisible. Remember that basic comfort and communication needs are valid. A small request can prevent resentment, withdrawal, or a bigger conflict later.

cards.title: Exercise: express your needs with DEAR MAN
cards.bodyMarkdown: Use this exercise when you want to explain a tinnitus-related need or ask for an accommodation. Describe the situation, express how it affects you, assert a clear request, and reinforce why it matters. Then use the MAN skills to stay focused, appear confident, and remain open to a workable compromise.

cards.title: Main points for communicating with others
cards.bodyMarkdown: Tinnitus can affect relationships, but skillful communication can reduce misunderstanding. DEAR MAN helps you make requests clearly. Small, respectful requests can prevent withdrawal and resentment. Communication is one way to stay engaged with life while still respecting what your ears and nervous system need.

cards.title: Confidence inside and outside
cards.bodyMarkdown: Supporting yourself and communicating with others are two sides of the same skill set. Internally, you practice validation and self-compassion so tinnitus does not become a reason to attack yourself. Externally, you practice clear requests so tinnitus does not push you into silence or isolation. Both help you stay engaged with life while continuing to use the tools that support you.

audio.transcript: Tinnitus is invisible, which means other people may not know what you are dealing with unless you explain it. modules.title: Sleep
modules.purpose: Sleep and tinnitus can affect each other, and small supports can reduce the pressure around rest.
modules.overviewMarkdown: Many people with tinnitus notice that nighttime can feel harder. Life is quieter, the day is over, and there may be fewer distractions from the sound. At the same time, poor sleep can make the next day feel heavier, increasing stress, frustration, and tinnitus distress. This section helps you understand that two-way relationship and gives you practical sleep-supportive steps without turning this app into a sleep-treatment program.

cards.title: What you will learn in this section
cards.bodyMarkdown: By the end of this section, you should understand how tinnitus and sleep can feed into each other, how negative sleep thoughts can increase bedtime anxiety, and why some bedtime habits accidentally make insomnia stronger. You will also learn how low-level sound, calmer sleep thoughts, basic sleep hygiene, and stimulus-control ideas can support better rest.

cards.title: Why sleep belongs in tinnitus management
cards.bodyMarkdown: Sleep may seem separate from tinnitus, but the two are often closely connected. When sleep is poor, your stress system has less time to recover, your attention may narrow, and difficult sounds can feel harder to ignore. When tinnitus feels threatening at bedtime, sleep can become harder to reach. That is why sleep belongs in a multimodal tinnitus plan.

cards.title: The sleep-tinnitus loop
cards.bodyMarkdown: A difficult night can lead to fatigue, irritability, and more worry the next day. That stress can make tinnitus feel more intrusive, especially when you are tired. Then, when bedtime returns, the memory of the previous bad night can make you anxious before you even lie down. This loop can feel powerful, but it also gives you several places to intervene.

cards.title: Why quiet nights can feel harder
cards.bodyMarkdown: Tinnitus often stands out when the environment becomes quiet. At night, there may be fewer external sounds, fewer tasks, and less social distraction. The brain can begin scanning for the ringing, buzzing, or hissing, and that attention can make the sound feel more important. This is one reason soft, steady background sound can be helpful at bedtime.
cards.safetyNote: Keep sound low, steady, and comfortable.

cards.title: Why trying harder to sleep can backfire
cards.bodyMarkdown: Sleep is unusual because effort does not always help. Trying to force sleep can make your mind more alert, especially if you start checking the clock, measuring the night, or predicting how bad tomorrow will be. The goal is not to work harder at sleeping. The goal is to create conditions where sleep is more likely to happen naturally.

cards.title: Sleep drive: your body’s pressure for sleep
cards.bodyMarkdown: Sleep drive is the natural pressure for sleep that builds the longer you are awake. When people spend too much time in bed awake, nap excessively, or go to bed much earlier to make up for a poor night, that pressure can weaken. A stronger sleep drive can make sleep more continuous and less fragile.
cards.safetyNote: Avoid rigid sleep restriction guidance in the app; direct persistent insomnia to professional care.

cards.title: When the bed becomes a place for frustration
cards.bodyMarkdown: If you lie awake night after night, the bed can start to feel connected with frustration, worry, clock-checking, and tinnitus monitoring. Your brain may learn that bed means wakefulness instead of sleep. Stimulus control is a behavioral sleep idea designed to rebuild the connection between bed and successful sleep.
cards.safetyNote: Frame as education; users with persistent insomnia should seek qualified sleep care.

cards.title: Stimulus control, explained carefully
cards.bodyMarkdown: In sleep treatment, stimulus control often means going to bed when sleepy, leaving bed if you are awake for a while, doing something quiet and relaxing, and returning when sleepiness returns. The point is not punishment, and it is not a test of willpower. It is a way of helping the brain relearn that bed is for sleep, not for hours of struggling.
cards.safetyNote: Educational only; not full CBT-I/BBTI. Users with complex sleep concerns should get help.

cards.title: Sleep thoughts can raise the alarm
cards.bodyMarkdown: Sleep-related thoughts can become convincing at night. Thoughts like “If I do not sleep eight hours, tomorrow is ruined” or “I will never fall asleep with tinnitus” can raise anxiety and make the body more alert. These thoughts may feel true in the moment, but they can often be checked and softened.

cards.title: Common sleep myths
cards.bodyMarkdown: Sleep myths create pressure. You may hear that everyone needs exactly eight hours, that one bad night ruins the next day, or that staying in bed awake will eventually force sleep. A more balanced view is usually more helpful: sleep needs vary, bad nights happen, and your body can often function better than your anxious mind predicts.

cards.title: Sleep myth examples
cards.bodyMarkdown: Examples of sleep myths include: “I must get eight hours or I will fail,” “I can always catch up on weekends,” “alcohol helps me sleep better,” “complete silence is best,” “if I stay in bed long enough I will force sleep,” and “more time in bed always means more rest.” Each of these has a more balanced version that lowers pressure.
cards.safetyNote: Avoid advice that contradicts clinician-directed sleep care.

cards.title: Using sound at night
cards.bodyMarkdown: Sound can help at night by reducing the contrast between silence and tinnitus. The sound should usually be low-level, steady, and comfortable. Loud, surprising, or highly varied sound may keep the brain more alert. The goal is not to create a perfect sound environment. The goal is to make the night feel less stark and less tinnitus-focused.
cards.safetyNote: Use safe, comfortable listening levels.

cards.title: Sleep hygiene is helpful, but it is not the whole answer
cards.bodyMarkdown: Sleep hygiene includes habits that support sleep: a consistent schedule, a calmer wind-down, less late caffeine, a comfortable bedroom, and fewer stimulating activities right before bed. These habits matter, but sleep hygiene alone may not fix insomnia. For many people, the bigger shift comes from changing the thoughts and behaviors that keep the bed connected with stress.

cards.title: A consistent schedule
cards.bodyMarkdown: A consistent sleep schedule helps your body clock predict when sleep and wakefulness should happen. A regular wake time is especially important, even after a rough night. This does not mean you must be rigid forever. It means giving your body repeated cues so the sleep system has a clearer rhythm.
cards.safetyNote: Users with unusual work schedules or medical conditions may need individualized advice.

cards.title: A wind-down routine
cards.bodyMarkdown: A wind-down routine gives the brain a transition. Reading, gentle stretching, quiet breathing, or calming audio can help signal that the day is ending. Try to avoid stressful work, intense conversations, or stimulating tasks right before bed when possible. The purpose is not to force sleep, but to lower the activation level around bedtime.

cards.title: The sleep environment
cards.bodyMarkdown: A bedroom that is cool, dark, comfortable, and low in disruption can make sleep easier. For tinnitus, “quiet” does not always mean silent. A soft, steady sound can be useful if silence makes tinnitus stand out. Try to keep the bed connected mainly with sleep, so your brain has a clear signal about what the space is for.
cards.safetyNote: Avoid uncomfortable or unsafe sound levels.

cards.title: Stimulants, food, alcohol, and activity
cards.bodyMarkdown: Caffeine and nicotine can make it harder to fall asleep or stay asleep, especially later in the day. Alcohol may feel relaxing at first, but it can fragment sleep later in the night. Heavy meals close to bedtime can be disruptive for some people. Regular movement can support sleep, while intense late workouts may be too activating for some.
cards.safetyNote: Medication/substance questions should be discussed with a clinician.

cards.title: Managing stress before bed
cards.bodyMarkdown: If worries or to-do lists flood in at night, try giving them another place to go earlier in the evening. Some people write down worries, next steps, or tomorrow’s tasks before the wind-down begins. Breathing, mindfulness, or paired muscle relaxation can also help the body shift out of problem-solving mode.

cards.title: Important terms
cards.bodyMarkdown: Stimulus control is the idea of rebuilding the connection between bed and sleep. Sleep drive is the pressure for sleep that builds while you are awake. Sleep distortions are rigid or threatening thoughts about sleep. Sleep hygiene is the set of habits and environmental choices that support healthier sleep.

cards.title: Putting sleep strategies into practice
cards.bodyMarkdown: Start with one or two realistic changes rather than trying everything at once. Notice your bedtime thoughts, choose a more balanced response, and consider whether your bed has become a place for worry. Keep sound low and steady if it helps. Choose one small adjustment you can practice consistently enough to learn from it.
cards.safetyNote: Persistent or severe insomnia warrants professional evaluation.

cards.title: CBT-I and brief behavioral sleep care
cards.bodyMarkdown: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia, often called CBT-I, is a structured treatment for insomnia. Brief Behavioral Treatment for Insomnia, or BBTI, is a shorter behavioral approach. This app does not provide either treatment. It introduces a few ideas that can help you understand your options and decide whether professional sleep support may be worth exploring. These programs can be good starting points to search for, if you need more help.
cards.safetyNote: Do not present as treatment; encourage sleep professional when appropriate.

cards.title: When sleep deserves professional help
cards.bodyMarkdown: Some sleep problems deserve more than self-guided education. Consider professional support if sleep problems are persistent, severe, worsening, or affecting safety, mood, work, or health. Suspected sleep apnea, loud snoring with breathing pauses, significant daytime sleepiness, complex medication questions, or ongoing insomnia are reasons to speak with a qualified clinician.
cards.safetyNote: Sleep apnea and severe insomnia should be assessed professionally.

cards.title: How sleep connects to the bigger picture
cards.bodyMarkdown: Better sleep can make it easier to think clearly, regulate emotions, practice sound therapy, use mindfulness, and communicate well. The strategies in this section mirror the rest of the app: notice patterns, check thoughts, make small behavioral changes, and avoid judging yourself for difficult nights. Sleep is part of resilience.

cards.title: FAQ: Should I stay in bed and force sleep?
cards.bodyMarkdown: Usually, forcing sleep makes things harder. Lying awake for long stretches can teach the brain that bed is a place for wakefulness and frustration. A calmer approach is to reduce the struggle, do something quiet if needed, and return when sleepiness comes back.
cards.safetyNote: Educational only; not prescriptive treatment.

cards.title: FAQ: Why am I still awake if I already use sleep hygiene?
cards.bodyMarkdown: Sleep hygiene is useful, but it is not always enough. If the main problem is worry, clock-checking, long periods awake in bed, or fear of tinnitus at night, then thought patterns and bedtime behaviors may need attention too.

cards.title: FAQ: Can I use TV or my phone to mask tinnitus?
cards.bodyMarkdown: TV or phone audio may feel helpful at first, but it can also be stimulating, bright, varied, or attention-grabbing. If you use sound at night, aim for soft, steady, neutral sound that supports rest rather than pulling your attention back into the screen or the story.
cards.safetyNote: Avoid unsafe volume and screen overuse.

cards.title: Practice: Challenge a negative sleep thought
cards.bodyMarkdown: Your thoughts about sleep can shape the experience of trying to rest. In this exercise, you write down a distressing sleep thought, identify the pattern, look at evidence for and against it, and create a more balanced statement. The goal is not to make the night perfect. The goal is to lower the alarm around sleep.

cards.title: Practice: Build a bedtime sound plan
cards.bodyMarkdown: A bedtime sound plan helps you decide what sound you will use, where it will come from, how comfortable the volume should be, and what you will do if it is not helping. A plan reduces last-minute problem-solving, which can be especially useful when tinnitus feels louder at night.
cards.safetyNote: Use low, comfortable, steady sound.

cards.title: Main points
cards.bodyMarkdown: Tinnitus can magnify insomnia, and poor sleep can make tinnitus distress harder to manage. Negative sleep thoughts can raise bedtime anxiety. Gentle sound, balanced thinking, consistent routines, and careful behavior changes can help break the cycle. Sleep strategies work best when they support rest without turning sleep into another performance test.

cards.title: Your sleep support plan
cards.bodyMarkdown: Before you move on, choose one small way to support sleep this week. You might use a low-level sound, write a more balanced sleep thought, start a gentler wind-down, or talk with a clinician about a sleep concern. Keep the step small enough to actually try.

cards.bodyMarkdown: Use this single-play sleep-oriented guided practice as a wind-down support. This is education and practice support, not sleep treatment.

audio.title: When sleep deserves professional help
audio.transcript: Some sleep problems deserve more than self-guided education. Consider professional support if sleep problems are persistent, severe, worsening, or affecting safety, mood, work, or health. Suspected sleep apnea, loud snoring with breathing pauses, significant daytime sleepiness, complex medication questions, or ongoing insomnia are reasons to speak with a qualified clinician.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: How sleep connects to the bigger picture
audio.transcript: Better sleep can make it easier to think clearly, regulate emotions, practice sound therapy, use mindfulness, and communicate well. The strategies in this section mirror the rest of the app: notice patterns, check thoughts, make small behavioral changes, and avoid judging yourself for difficult nights. Sleep is part of resilience.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: FAQ: Should I stay in bed and force sleep?
audio.transcript: Usually, forcing sleep makes things harder. Lying awake for long stretches can teach the brain that bed is a place for wakefulness and frustration. A calmer approach is to reduce the struggle, do something quiet if needed, and return when sleepiness comes back.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: FAQ: Why am I still awake if I already use sleep hygiene?
audio.transcript: Sleep hygiene is useful, but it is not always enough. If the main problem is worry, clock-checking, long periods awake in bed, or fear of tinnitus at night, then thought patterns and bedtime behaviors may need attention too.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: FAQ: Can I use TV or my phone to mask tinnitus?
audio.transcript: TV or phone audio may feel helpful at first, but it can also be stimulating, bright, varied, or attention-grabbing. If you use sound at night, aim for soft, steady, neutral sound that supports rest rather than pulling your attention back into the screen or the story.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Practice: Challenge a negative sleep thought
audio.transcript: Your thoughts about sleep can shape the experience of trying to rest. In this exercise, you write down a distressing sleep thought, identify the pattern, look at evidence for and against it, and create a more balanced statement. The goal is not to make the night perfect. The goal is to lower the alarm around sleep.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Practice: Build a bedtime sound plan
audio.transcript: A bedtime sound plan helps you decide what sound you will use, where it will come from, how comfortable the volume should be, and what you will do if it is not helping. A plan reduces last-minute problem-solving, which can be especially useful when tinnitus feels louder at night.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Main points
audio.transcript: Tinnitus can magnify insomnia, and poor sleep can make tinnitus distress harder to manage. Negative sleep thoughts can raise bedtime anxiety. Gentle sound, balanced thinking, consistent routines, and careful behavior changes can help break the cycle. Sleep strategies work best when they support rest without turning sleep into another performance test.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Your sleep support plan
audio.transcript: Before you move on, choose one small way to support sleep this week. You might use a low-level sound, write a more balanced sleep thought, start a gentler wind-down, or talk with a clinician about a sleep concern. Keep the step small enough to actually try.
audio.playbackContext: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio.title: Sleep scope and safety
audio.transcript: This section provides sleep education, not diagnosis or treatment. If sleep problems are persistent, severe, worsening, or connected to symptoms such as breathing pauses, heavy snoring, major daytime sleepiness, unsafe thoughts, or major mood changes, seek professional support. Do not stop or change prescribed sleep medication based on this app.

modules.overviewMarkdown: My Plan collects the exercises, tools, statements, and short practices that feel useful to you. It is not a scorecard and it is not a treatment plan. It is a local place to keep the pieces you want to return to.

cards.title: What belongs in My Plan
cards.bodyMarkdown: Use My Plan for practice tools you want to repeat: a sound plan, a breathing exercise, a Yes AND statement, a thought-reframing exercise, or a communication script. Ordinary education cards do not need to be saved unless they become a practice tool for you.

cards.title: Three Lines Journal
cards.bodyMarkdown: The Three Lines Journal keeps practice small, and can create a daily routine. ST stands for Sound Therapy, E stands for Emotional Regulation, and M stands for Mindfulness. A few words, a checkmark, or 'not today' can be enough.

cards.title: The point is reflection, not proof
cards.bodyMarkdown: Three Lines is not meant to become a black hole of journaling. If one line is blank, notice it without judgment. If the same line is blank for several days, that may show low-hanging fruit the next time we are looking for patterns in tinnitus.

cards.title: Past entries and exercise records
cards.bodyMarkdown: When you save journal entries or exercise responses, they stay on this device so you can look back later. Reviewing old entries can help you notice patterns, repeated tools, and areas that may need more attention.
